title: Region-dependent regulation of Tau phosphorylation by Glycerophosphodiester Phosphodiesterase 2 in a mouse model of tauopathy
abstract: Hyperphosphorylation of Tau promotes its aggregation and neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) formation, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and neurodegeneration in diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and AD-related dementias (ADRDs). However, the mechanisms underlying dysregulated Tau phosphorylation under pathological contexts remain unclear. Glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 2 (GDE2) is a six-transmembrane enzyme that acts at the cell surface to cleave the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor that tethers a subclass of proteins to the membrane. Here, we show that in the PS19 tauopathy mouse model, GDE2 disruption modulates Tau phosphorylation by transiently decreasing Tau's propensity for aggregation through region-specific regulation of local kinase environments. In the cortex, GDE2 ablation in 6-month-old PS19 male mice (PS19;Gde2KO) reduces Tau phosphorylation at Serine (S)202/Threonine (T)205, T212, and S396 but increases S262 phosphorylation in the hippocampus of 6-month-old PS19;Gde2KO male and female mice. Consistent with these changes, in males, Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3  / {beta} (GSK3  / {beta}) activity is decreased in the cortex, while AKT activity is increased in both males and females in the hippocampus, with no changes in protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) activity. Primary cortical neurons from PS19;Gde2KO animals showed reduced Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, implying cell-autonomous roles for neuronal GDE2 in this process. GDE2 overexpression in heterologous SH-SY5Y cells increased Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, while a catalytically inactive form of GDE2 did not, suggesting that GDE2 regulation of target GPI-anchored protein surface activity is required to modulate Tau phosphorylation. Taken together, our study identifies GDE2 as a component of the complex regulatory network that controls Tau phosphorylation in the context of tauopathy and provides insight into putative pathways relevant to Tau pathologies observed in disease.

title: Sensory neurons gate a cortical plasticity window for immune encoding
abstract: Activity-dependent plasticity allows brain circuits to encode experience, but this has been established with brief stimuli. Immune responses develop over days and are represented in the insular cortex (IC). How the cortex encodes experiences with this temporal structure is unknown. Here we show that Trpv1+ sensory neurons open a multi-day cortical plasticity window matched to the immune response. Following peripheral immune challenges, Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons are activated first, restricting plasticity. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons respond two days later, disinhibiting IC excitatory neurons. Weaker challenges trigger the first phase but not the second, and preventing the transition blocks immune encoding, whereas lowering inhibition beforehand does not. These results identify a body-to-brain mechanism that gates cortical plasticity on the timescale of slowly evolving physiological experience.

title: Sensory recurrence and convergent integration in the C. elegans connectome
abstract: The synaptic wiring of Caenorhabditis elegans has a global feed-forward architecture, from sensory to motor neurons. Yet, whole-brain optogenetic mapping shows that signals do not flow predominantly forward, and sensory neurons respond to more neurons than they drive. Where the wiring contains pathways leading back to their starting point is unclear. Here, we locate this recurrence using the feedback coefficient, derived from the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger framework for directed networks, which quantifies the proportion of walks reaching a neuron that originate from itself. The connectome has about three times more recurrence than strength-matched random networks, with the largest excess in sensory neurons, whereas random wiring places it on highly connected neurons. Along the thermotaxis pathway, this produces a recurrence gradient from thermosensory neurons to integrating interneurons. The ordering replicates in five reconstructions, including two independent adults, persists when reciprocal contacts are preserved or gap junctions removed, but vanishes with only short paths or loop counts. Convergence shows the reverse pattern, with every neuron receiving walks from fewer sources than in random wiring, especially sensory neurons. The wiring extends from a sensory periphery folding back on itself to interneurons and motor neurons integrating many sources, a candidate structural substrate for non-feed-forward signalling.

title: Socio-demographic gradients in traumatic brain injury disability, severity and nutrition: a two-level analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 and NHANES 2011-2014
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is among the most consequential non-fatal outcomes of trauma, yet how its burden, severity and nutritional context are patterned by socio-demographic development remains incompletely characterised. We addressed this question at two levels. Using the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study 2023, we quantified the socio-demographic gradients of TBI disability across the five socio-demographic index (SDI) quintiles and characterised the severity composition of the TBI disability burden, its 1990-2023 trend and its cause-specific structure. Using pooled NHANES 2011-2014, we then examined, at the individual level, how reported TBI history among US adults aged 40 years and older varied by income, education, health insurance and food security, and whether dietary differences between adults with and without a TBI history persisted after socio-economic adjustment. The age-standardised TBI disability rate was almost twice as high in the high SDI quintile as in the low SDI quintile (113.68 versus 57.55 per 100,000 in 2023), a gap essentially unchanged since 1990. Moderate or severe injuries accounted for 72.5% of the TBI disability burden in the high SDI quintile versus 84.0-84.6% in the other four quintiles, rising in every quintile between 1990 and 2023. Among US adults, reported TBI history rose with educational attainment (11.9% below high school versus 17.3% above) and was most common in very food-insecure households (23.4%; adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.39-2.09); income showed no unadjusted gradient but a negative association after mutual adjustment. Unadjusted dietary differences between adults with and without a TBI history largely attenuated after socio-economic adjustment, with only fibre density remaining marginally lower (-0.35 g/1,000 kcal, 95% confidence interval -0.64 to -0.06). The moderate or severe share of the disability burden is a tractable, mortality-free monitoring indicator for injury prevention, and nutritional risk among food-insecure TBI survivors warrants clinical attention.

title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and 2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Results Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by 1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced 2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Conclusions Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.

title: Stable large-scale network architecture and structured individual variability in the awake mouse brain
abstract: Large-scale functional networks provide a scaffold for brain activity, but their population architecture and inter-individual variability remain poorly defined in the awake mouse brain. Here we introduce the Awake Mouse Connectome Project (AMCP), a population-scale multimodal MRI resource comprising 212 sex-balanced awake mice. Using this dataset, we generated high-precision in vivo tissue probability maps, derived a reproducible whole-brain functional network atlas and quantified structured variability in network connectivity across animals. The resulting atlas defined a stable large-scale architecture aligned with structural topology, while inter-individual functional connectivity variability followed organized connectional gradients rather than random dispersion. We further benchmarked the clustering-derived scaffold against conventional group independent component analysis (GICA) and release the GICA network atlas as an accompanying resource. AMCP further provides empirical scaling relationships linking sample size, scan duration and connectome precision. These analyses indicate that mean functional connectivity and functional connectivity variability have distinct sample-size requirements, providing a protocol-specific guidance for studies focused on group-average connectivity and inter-individual variability. Individualized network parcellations derived from the AMCP scaffold improved behavioural prediction relative to group-average features for selected behavioural domains, indicating functional relevance of subject-specific network architecture. Together, AMCP establishes an open dataset, tissue-template resource, clustering-derived and GICA functional atlases, and analysis toolbox for reproducible awake mouse connectomics and for translational studies linking circuit mechanisms to large-scale brain organization.

title: State-dependent emergence of coupling between oscillatory and aperiodic neural activity
abstract: Neural oscillations and aperiodic activity are two quintessential mesoscopic-level features arising from shared circuits, yet what governs their relationship remains unclear. Here we show that coupling between oscillatory frequency and aperiodic exponent is sporadic and state-dependent. Bias-reduced analyses of 3,245 intracranial contacts from 61 awake subjects showed significant coupling in only <13% of contacts per band. A connectome-constrained dynamical model predicted that neither changes of input to local circuit nor removal of long-range connections modulated the coupling; whereas stronger local inhibitory feedback drove covariation between oscillatory frequency and aperiodic exponent. The model predictions were supported by three independent experiments: transcranial stimulation shifted each component independently and focal ablation of remote cortical tissues did not change coupling; whereas coupling emerged during seizures that altered local excitatory-inhibitory balance. These results suggest that the relation between periodic and aperiodic neural activity is neither intrinsically independent nor coupled, but determined by local circuit states.

title: Strategy-dependent causal relationships between large-scale cortical activity and perceptual decisions
abstract: Animals can adopt different internally generated strategies to solve decision-making tasks, but whether cortical regions distinctly contribute to decisions under different strategies remains unknown. To address this problem, we analyzed three datasets comprising either cortical widefield imaging, or optogenetic inactivation of dozens of cortical locations in 54 mice, all performing the same sensory-evidence-accumulation task. Using Generalized Linear Model-Hidden Markov Models (GLM-HMMs), we found that the mice adopted one of three underlying strategies: an engaged, stimulus-driven state, and two disengaged states characterized by large side biases. The specific effects of inactivation of cortical regions depended on behavioral strategy: during engaged states, inactivation tended to increase side bias, while the opposite was true in biased states. For engaged states, these effects were most prominent when frontal regions were inactivated. Moreover, neural decoding analyses from cortex-wide activity revealed that frontal regions preferentially encode the animals' choices during engaged states relative to biased states. Our results suggest that distinct patterns of large-scale cortical dynamics underlie decisions under different task strategies and identify the frontal cortex as an important substrate of engaged-strategy control.

title: Striatal and frontal signatures of social context and cost-benefit decision making in developmental stuttering
abstract: Developmental stuttering is usually framed as a sensorimotor disorder, yet it manifests in communicative situations that engage motivational, self-referential, and regulatory processes. In this case-control study, we combined a socio-economic decision task outside the scanner with a socially modulated speech task during functional MRI to test how listener presence and self-referential speech shape neural activity in 34 adults who stutter and 32 controls. Both groups valued talking with another person about themselves more than talking with another person about someone else or talking to themselves. On the neural level, listener-directed (vs. private) speech and self-disclosure (vs. guessing the preferences of a famous other) elicited stronger responses in the ventral striatum and medial prefrontal cortex, with no significant group differences in the central listener-directed versus private contrast. Within the stuttering group, individual differences revealed a systematic reweighting of socially modulated activation as a function of symptom burden: higher anticipation of stuttering and greater self-reported impact of stuttering on everyday life were associated with stronger engagement of motivational circuitry, greater recruitment of frontal evaluative-control regions, and reduced contextual differentiation within speech-language cortex. Stuttering anticipation and lived experience gradually shift the balance between control, language, and motivational salience-processing systems, contributing to the disorder's marked heterogeneity and context sensitivity. These findings indicate system-level signatures of the interaction between social context and symptom severity in developmental stuttering, extending accounts based on sensorimotor deficits.

title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes
abstract: Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators (R1-R5). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1, R2, R3, and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1-R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

title: Summed contrasts can conceal reversed regional preferences: directional and dose criteria for screening transcranial direct current stimulation montage pairs
abstract: Background: The regional-matching design evaluated here requires two transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) montages, each stronger in its own target region, with adequate exposure. Summed contrasts can be positive when only one preference holds. Objective: To test whether a summed double-dissociation index (DDI), overlap and cohort-median dose rules identify such pairs, for a focused-attention versus open-monitoring experiment. Methods: Twenty-four montage pairs were simulated in 20 anatomical head models (SimNIBS 4.6, 2 mA). A four-rule screen (DDI, overlap, cohort-median dose) was recorded before cohort results; a post hoc conjunction required both regional contrasts positive in >=80% of heads. Two leading pairs were compared on per-head dose, a second solver and 60 conductivity stress-test draws. Results: Eighteen pairs passed the screen, but 13 failed the conjunction; one with positive median DDI (0.782) reversed the salience-region preference in all 20 heads. The nominated pair (F3-centered 4x1 ring; F8-Fp2 sponges; median DDI 1.561; both preferences in 20/20 heads) brought both anatomical targets to the 0.20 V/m operational floor in 11/20 heads; a conventional sponge pair (DDI 0.627) did so in 20/20, though both passed the cohort-median dose rule. The nominated pair's separation held across a second solver and all 60 stress-test draws, but both network targets reached the floor in 19/60. Conclusions: Summed indices and cohort-median dose rules can pass pairs that fail reciprocal-exposure criteria. Such screens should pre-specify the directional conjunction and report per-head joint dose coverage. These are modeled exposures, not physiological or behavioral effects.

title: Surprisal contributes little beyond contextual embeddings in high-gamma ECoG encoding
abstract: Surprisal and contextual embeddings are both derived from large language models and are widely used to predict neural responses during language comprehension, but it is unclear whether surprisal adds information beyond embeddings. We test this directly: does word surprisal improve out-of-sample prediction of high-gamma ECoG responses after GPT-2 XL contextual embeddings are included? Using public ECoG recordings from natural speech, we fit word-aligned ridge encoding models with baseline stimulus features, GPT-2 XL embeddings, and GPT-2 XL surprisal. Adding one surprisal predictor left held-out correlation essentially unchanged at the primary response window, and the increment stayed within an equivalence margin across alternative lags, residualized surprisal, and frequency-band targets; it did not uniformly meet the same criterion under banded ridge regularization or within labeled temporal subsets. This small increment suggests that surprisal does not act as an independent predictor. It is better understood as a compressed readout of the same broader predictive state that the embeddings already capture.

title: Systematic Spike Sorting Errors Revealed by Juxtacellular Ground Truth in the Awake Brain
abstract: Existing ground-truth data for spike sorting come almost entirely from anesthetized or in vitro preparations. Yet phenomena expected to challenge spike sorting most (spike overlap and bursting) depend on brain state and differ in the awake brain. Therefore, error estimates from existing benchmarks may not transfer to awake recordings, and the types of errors in the awake brain remain largely uncharacterized. To address this, we generated a ground-truth dataset (16 neurons) using paired juxtacellular-extracellular electrophysiology in awake mice, and found spike sorting performance, particularly recall, to be lower than conventional benchmarks might suggest. Generally, false negatives sharply increased with intrinsic physiological factors like bursting, whereas false positives were more strongly associated with extrinsic factors, such as putative spike overlaps. To quantify contributions to errors from intrinsic and extrinsic factors, for each observed juxtacellular waveform we predicted the corresponding extracellular waveform. In the best-performing sorter, we estimate approximately half of false positives were attributable to credulous attempts to resolve putative overlaps. Bursting and putative overlaps were each associated with a roughly doubled false negative rate when they occurred separately, and with a sevenfold increase when they occurred together. These co-occurrences accounted for approximately 40% of a typical neuron's false negatives, despite comprising only approximately a fifth of its spikes. Thus, the moments when spike sorters must rely on the assumption of waveform invariance the most to resolve overlaps are exactly the moments when bursting makes that assumption least valid. We also estimate that three-quarters of false negatives had been detected but assigned to other units. These spikes were not cleanly oversplit: post-hoc merging was not productive because the loss in precision was three times the gain in recall. Because bursting and spike overlaps often co-occur, sorting spikes by waveform similarity and repairing the result by post hoc merging is unlikely to adequately balance precision and recall in the situations of greatest scientific interest. That is, while bursting and spike overlaps may involve only a minority of spikes, the resulting sorting errors may disproportionately distort the interpretation of neuronal population dynamics. We thus conclude that uncertainty quantification in sorters' output is essential.

title: TRPV4 antagonist efficacy in a post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus pig model
abstract: Hydrocephalus occurs across the age spectrum but is particularly prevalent in young and old individuals. One form of this disease is post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH), which is a life-threatening sequela of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). There are no effective non-surgical interventions for the treatment of PHH or other forms of hydrocephalus. Progress has been limited by the lack of gyrencephalic animal models that exhibit high fidelity to human conditions. Here, we establish a pathophysiologically relevant novel swine model of IVH that recapitulates key features of severe PHH, including sustained ventriculomegaly, elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), neuroinflammation and white matter injury. Using this model, we test the therapeutic potential of pharmacologic inhibition of the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) non-specific cationic channel. The orally bioavailable TRPV4 antagonist GSK2789917 penetrates the blood-brain barrier, and prevents progression to PHH when administered 2 days after IVH. Specifically, GSK2789917 prevents the development of ventriculomegaly, suppresses early ICP elevations and prevents or reverses inflammasome activation. These findings establish a clinically relevant large-animal model of PHH and identify TRPV4 antagonism as a promising treatment for hydrocephalus.

title: The anti-dyskinetic and the anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine are also present in female preclinical models
abstract: Biological sex is an important determinant of neuropharmacological response, yet females remain underrepresented in preclinical studies of Parkinson's disease (PD) and L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). We previously demonstrated that sub-anesthetic ketamine reduces established LID, attenuates dyskinesia development, and produces anti-parkinsonian effects in male unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) rat models. However, whether these therapeutic effects extend to females remained unknown. Here, we evaluated the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine in female Sprague-Dawley rats using the attenuation and established models of LID. In the attenuation paradigm, unilateral 6-OHDA-lesioned females received repeated L-DOPA administration with either ketamine (20 mg/kg, i.p.; 10-h dosing paradigm) or vehicle. Ketamine significantly attenuated the progressive development of dyskinesia, indicating that early intervention modified the trajectory of LID expression. In the established LID paradigm, ketamine produced robust significant acute reductions in abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs) after dyskinesia had fully developed, and these significant effects persisted for up to 49 days following treatment, demonstrating sustained suppression of dyskinesia severity. To determine whether ketamine altered therapeutic motor function, forelimb adjusting steps testing was performed in female unilateral 6-OHDA rats. Ketamine did not impair L-DOPA-mediated motor improvement suggesting compatibility with the gold standard medication. Ketamine was also by itself associated with significantly improved stepping performance during ketamine treatment conditions, indicating acute anti-parkinsonian motor benefit. Together, these findings demonstrate that the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of ketamine extend to female preclinical models and strengthen the translational rationale for repurposing sub-anesthetic ketamine as a potential therapeutic strategy for individuals with LID.

title: Topographic reference modelling of white matter hyperintensities across the adult lifespan
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are among the most common MRI findings in older adults. They are widely regarded as markers of brain aging and cerebral small-vessel disease, and associated with risk for cognitive decline, Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD), and stroke. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are typically interpreted by total lesion burden, but lesions with similar volumes can occupy different anatomical locations, potentially reflecting distinct pathological processes. Here we present voxelwise topographic reference modelling (vTRM), a framework for characterizing individual WMH masks against age- and sex-stratified frequency maps derived from cognitively unimpaired individuals. Using 42,469 FLAIR-derived lesion masks from twelve adult cohorts, we mapped population-level WMH spatial vulnerability, characterized age-related changes in its distribution across periventricular, lobar and arterial-territory compartments, and constructed paired percentile charts for lesion burden and spatial typicality. A quadrant-based classification defined by these two percentile dimensions revealed graded relationships with ADRD pathophysiology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, while identifying WMH patterns differentially associated with ageing-related, vascular and neurodegenerative processes among individuals with similar lesion volumes. These reference charts establish a benchmark for normative WMH ageing, enabling quantification of individual deviations from typical age-, sex- and burden-related patterns and identification of WMH phenotypes associated with vascular, neurodegenerative or mixed etiologies. The framework, together with a deployable 3D U-Net model trained on these data for automated WMH segmentation, is available through the Brain Lesion Analytics platform (https://brainlesionanalytics.org/).

title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation reverses adolescent alcohol-induced cellular and behavioral deficits.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol is commonly consumed by adolescents in a binge-like pattern that can produce persistent cognitive impairments. Previous work found that adolescent intermittent ethanol (AIE) exposure reduces parvalbumin expressing (PV+) interneurons and increases perineuronal net (PNN) expression in brain regions critical for cognition. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for treating psychiatric disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether AIE exposure alters PV+ interneurons and PNN expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and impairs cognition, and whether mPFC-targeted gamma tACS can reverse these effects. METHODS: Sprague Dawley rats (N=139, 50% female) underwent AIE or control exposure during adolescence and received Active or Sham mPFC-targeted gamma tACS treatment for three consecutive days in adulthood. Following stimulation, rats either underwent immunohistochemical assessment of PV+ and PNN expression or behavioral testing using the novel object recognition (NOR) task. RESULTS: AIE exposure reduced PV+ cell counts in the prelimbic cortex, an effect that was reversed by active tACS. In contrast, AIE exposure did not alter PNN measures. Interestingly, active tACS affected the prelimbic and infralimbic cortices more than the anterior cingulate cortex. AIE exposure also reduced recognition memory of a novel object, and this deficit was ameliorated by active tACS when assessed one week after stimulation. Additionally, active stimulation decreased anxiety-like behavior in the open-field test. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these results confirm that adolescent alcohol exposure produces lasting cellular and cognitive alterations and supports mPFC-targeted gamma tACS as a potential intervention for alcohol-induced dysfunction.

title: Transplantation of human iPSC-derived retinal cells in the cone-dominant Northern tree shrew
abstract: Abstract: Purpose: To characterize the transplantation and survival of photoreceptors generated from human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids in the Northern tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri, TS). Methods: TS eyes were injected with retinal cells dissociated from GFP-expressing hiPSC-derived retinal organoids (12 animals; n=22 eyes). 15 eyes had prior damage induced by either experimental retinal detachment (n=11) or ATP-induced retinal damage (n=4), and seven eyes were undamaged. Retinal organoids were treated with Notch pathway inhibitor 2 days before transplant. TS retinal structure and cellular details were assessed post-transplantation for up to 8 weeks using scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and adaptive optics SLO (AOSLO). Histological analysis was done at the end of the experiment. Results: Cell transplants in eyes treated with a simple immunosuppression treatment failed to survive for more than 2 weeks (n=10 eyes). Robust cell survival was observed in the eyes treated with a complex immunosuppression cocktail for up to 8 weeks (n=12 eyes). The transplanted cells were confirmed to be subretinally located using OCT imaging and the cell fate was confirmed to be human photoreceptors by histology. Finally, AOSLO imaging captured structures resembling photoreceptor inner segments. Conclusions: Our results demonstrate survival of transplanted cells using a species-specific immunosuppression treatment. Future studies should aim to explore the long-term survival and function of the transplanted cells.

title: Turning an object into a scene: buildings activate scene-selective visual cortex independently of visual features
abstract: Human visual cortex contains regions that selectively respond to both scenes and large objects, particularly buildings. The cortical overlap between buildings and scenes has been attributed to shared visual features (e.g., cardinal orientations, rectilinearity). Alternative accounts propose that buildings may also activate scene representations indirectly, independently of specific visual features, for example because buildings evoke a sense of space. Here, we tested for such feature-independent activation by comparing EEG and fMRI responses in human participants (both sexes) to buildings and visually-matched boxes, and relating these responses to scene-selective responses. Buildings and boxes were matched using image-based metrics, deep neural networks, and a perceptual similarity task. Time-resolved EEG decoding showed that buildings and boxes evoked discriminable responses from 360ms post-stimulus onset, incompatible with feedforward visual feature processing. Importantly, the building-box classifier generalized to discriminate scenes from chairs, providing the first EEG evidence for a representational overlap between buildings and scenes. Temporal generalization analyses further showed that the late building-selective response corresponded to an earlier scene-selective response, with a temporal offset of ~130ms. Finally, ultra-fast fMRI (TR=140ms) revealed that the scene-selective parahippocampal place area (PPA) similarly showed a feature-independent building-selective response that was delayed and prolonged relative to the scene-selective response. These results clarify the nature of building selectivity in visual cortex by showing that this selectivity is feature-independent and delayed relative to scene selectivity. We propose that intrinsic associations between object categories (e.g., buildings and scenes, tools and hands) may account for part of the categorical organization of ventral temporal cortex.

title: Ultradeep optical coherence tomography
abstract: Deep optical imaging of intact brain tissue is limited by scattering and absorption, restricting our ability to study subcortical structures. Here, we introduce ultradeep optical coherence tomography (OCT), which combines hardware and computational approaches to enhance the signal from deep tissue regions. Ultradeep OCT utilizes a longer illumination center wavelength of 1575 nm, spectral-domain balanced detection and imaging in the conjugate configuration with the zero optical path difference positioned deep in the tissue. Autocorrelation artifacts are measured and subtracted, and multiple frames are coherently averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio further. These techniques, along with computational refocusing and bandwidth control, allowed us to extend structural imaging depth in biological tissues. Ultradeep OCT demonstrated physical imaging depths of 2.3 to 2.8 mm (mean 2.5 mm) in the ex vivo mouse brain and 2.5 to 3.0 mm (mean 2.8 mm) in chicken tissue. The resulting volumes in the ex vivo mouse brain samples depict the dorsal hippocampus and its two major subregions with sufficient contrast to allow segmentation and three-dimensional reconstructions. Features in the thalamus could also be discerned. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultradeep OCT as a label-free approach for visualizing deep-brain structures at a spatial scale complementary to magnetic resonance imaging and microscopy. This approach could enable optical imaging studies of hippocampal structural changes in mouse models of neurodegenerative disease.

title: Unpredictable chronic stress redistributes novelty-evoked exploratory space use and yields method-dependent identification of resilient-like archetypes in zebrafish
abstract: Unpredictable chronic stress (UCS) produces heterogeneous behavioural outcomes, but identifying resilient individuals remains challenging because post-stress behaviour is multidimensional and classification depends on the analytical framework. We characterised novelty-evoked exploration in 178 adult zebrafish (89 unstressed reference, 89 UCS-exposed) using four Novel Tank Test variables: distance travelled, line crossings, upper-zone entries and upper-zone time, from a historical LAPCOM dataset from four independent cohorts. Behaviour was robustly normalised to control distributions within cohorts. In the unstressed population, principal component analysis revealed a dominant exploratory gradient (PC1 = 74.9%; PC2 = 18.7%), whereas weighted k-nearest-neighbour Louvain analysis yielded a stable two-profile partition. However, null-model inference and resampling did not support discrete behavioural populations, indicating a predominantly continuous reference architecture. UCS significantly redistributed individuals within this architecture (PERMANOVA: F(1,173) = 8.10, R2= 0.0423, p = 0.0016), reducing occupancy of the higher-exploration reference profile from 55.1% to 24.7%, while multivariate dispersion, Mahalanobis distance and global correlation structure showed no detectable differences. De novo Louvain analysis identified lower- and higher-exploration configurations, but correspondence with the control reference was asymmetric: all 44 lower-exploration fish mapped to the lower reference profile, whereas only 22 of 45 higher-exploration fish mapped to the higher reference profile. Thus, higher exploration after UCS was insufficient to define a resilient-like response. Across five analytical frameworks, resilient assignments ranged from 9 to 45 individuals and susceptible assignments from 23 to 68, with partial individual-level convergence. These findings support reference-integrated behavioural stratification for identifying resilient- and susceptible-like candidates for physiological, cellular and molecular validation.

title: Visual-cortex-projecting neurons in mouse auditory cortex show distinct audiovisual responses independent of motor-related activity
abstract: Cells in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) not only respond to visual stimulation, but also to sound. Part of this auditory modulation likely originates from auditory cortex (AC). Yet, the circuit-level functionality of the AC-to-V1 projection remains poorly understood. Here we performed acute in vivo high-density recordings in mouse AC during auditory, visual, and audiovisual stimulation, identifying AC-to-V1 projecting neurons by optogenetic tagging. Compared to non-tagged neurons, AC-to-V1 neurons more often responded to auditory, visual, or audiovisual stimuli. Furthermore, most AC-to-V1 neurons responded to specific sound frequencies; a modest but significant fraction was selective for visual orientations. These results could not be explained by motor responses or single-neuron variations in firing rate, cortical recording depth, or waveform type. These findings show that AC-to-V1 neurons carry sensory-specific signals, as opposed to nonspecific modulations, and exhibit distinctive response profiles compared to non-tagged AC neurons.

title: Why probe registration is crucial for infant fNIRS and HD-DOT? An evaluation across 49 newborns
abstract: Source-detector probe registration, i.e., the mapping of optode positions on the scalp to their true anatomical locations in head/brain space, is crucial for brain imaging with fNIRS or HD-DOT. While individual, MRI-based registration is desirable, it is not always feasible, motivating the development of alternative registration approaches. This study uses the STORM-Net registration protocol and quantifies the variation of cap alignment in a cohort of 49 newborns to evaluate how this affects reconstructed images using HD-DOT. Relative to a centrally aligned template, the cohort showed a median probe-position error of 10.12 mm, while the least and most misaligned subjects exhibited mean errors of 4.41 mm and 20.60 mm, respectively. The results demonstrate that the level of cap misalignment typically observed in newborn imaging can affect the spatial accuracy of reconstructed functional images, particularly in cases with larger probe displacements. These findings provide a quantitative basis for adopting more conservative interpretations of group-level functional brain activity and functional connectivity results, and strongly support the routine use of registration methods in infant HD-DOT studies.

title: Wolffia globosa -derived nanovesicles as a natural source of bioactive metabolites with neuroprotective potential against methylglyoxal-induced oxidative stress
abstract: Plant-derived nanovesicles (PDNVs) have attracted increasing attention for their potential biomedical applications, particularly in oxidative stress-related diseases and neuroprotection. Wolffia globosa, an emerging functional food and potential future food source, is rich in phytochemicals associated with health-promoting properties. Harnessing W. globosa-derived nanovesicles (WGNVs) represents a promising strategy for expanding the biomedical applications of this plant. In this study, WGNVs were isolated and characterized, and their neuroprotective potential was evaluated in vitro. The isolated WGNVs exhibited nanoscale dimensions and a lipid bilayer structure. Biochemical analyses revealed substantial total phenolic and flavonoid contents, alongside intrinsic antioxidant activities. Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified a diverse repertoire of metabolites, including major constituents subsequently validated using independent analytical approaches. These findings provided a foundation for investigating the neuroprotective effects of WGNVs in a methylglyoxal (MGX)-induced model of neuronal oxidative stress. High-resolution confocal microscopy demonstrated the cellular localization of WGNVs within neuronal cells, providing evidence of interactions between plant-derived nanovesicles and neuronal cells. WGNV treatment attenuated MGX-induced free radical accumulation and oxidative stress responses while preserving cellular morphology integrity. Collectively, this study provides foundational evidence of the physicochemical characteristics, metabolite composition, and in vitro neuroprotective potential of WGNVs. These findings highlight WGNVs as a promising naturally derived nanocarrier platform for investigating plant-animal interkingdom interactions and exploring potential therapeutic applications across a broad range of biomedical fields.

abstract: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

abstract: Insect olfaction is facilitated by a heterotetrameric odorant receptor-odorant receptor co-receptor (OR-Orco) complex. However, extensive sequence divergence and lineage-specific expansion have complicated large-scale comparisons of OR repertoires across insects. Here, we integrated sequence similarity, structural similarity, and molecular docking to analyze ORs from 115 insect species. OR repertoire size was associated with adult diet, larval diet, and habitat, but not with circadian rhythm. We developed a 'trunk-branch' network framework to classify ORs according to sequence and structural similarity and used large-scale molecular docking to derive comparative docking profiles. Despite marked differences in sequence- and structural-community composition, almost all sampled orders contained ORs assigned to all six docking-profile communities. Holometabolous insects showed higher OR sequence-community diversity than non-holometabolous insects, and docking-profile composition differed between extant lineages whose order-level origins predate or postdate the end-Permian mass extinction. Most notably, we identified a highly conserved extracellular β-sheet in Orco that restricts ligand access to the binding pocket and may contribute to its reduced capacity to bind natural odorants. The emergence of Orco represents a key evolutionary transition from homomeric receptors to heteromeric OR-Orco complexes, and our results suggest that this transition may have been accompanied by pronounced specialization of the extracellular domain and binding pocket. Together, these analyses provide a class-wide framework for comparing insect OR diversity and generate testable hypotheses for future experimental and evolutionary studies.

abstract: Tumorigenesis typically follows a multi-hit trajectory, driven by accumulating oncogenic mutations. Colorectal cancer (CRC) has long served as a paradigmatic model of multi-hit tumorigenesis, characterized by adenoma-carcinoma transition accompanied by acquisition of specific oncogene and tumor suppressor mutations. However, how the temporal order of early mutations influences CRC initiation remains poorly understood. To address this, we established a CRC tumorigenesis model using murine intestinal organoids. By introducing defined combinations of key CRC driver mutations ( Kras , Apc , and Trp53 ) in distinct orders, we systematically investigated how the order of mutation accumulation affects tumor initiation. Our results reveal that the mutation accumulation confers growth advantages in both in vitro and in vivo models. Strikingly, mutation order also influenced the tumorigenic properties of the organoids. Whereas organoids with Trp53 loss before or after Apc loss similarly affected organoid phenotypes in vitro or tumorigenicity in immunodeficient mice, organoids with Trp53 loss preceding Apc inactivation exhibited reduced tumor-forming potential in immunocompetent mice, likely due to their distinct immunological features. Collectively, our study reveals a critical role of ordered mutation accumulation in CRC initiation, an insight that may hold clinical relevance.

title: Spyglass is a framework for reproducible and shareable neuroscience research.
abstract: Scientific progress depends on reliable and reproducible results. Progress can be accelerated when data are shared and re-analyzed to address new questions. Current approaches to storing and analyzing neural data involve bespoke formats and software that make replication and reuse of data difficult. To address these challenges, we created Spyglass, an open-source data management and analysis framework written in Python. Spyglass provides reproducible pipelines for common neuroscience analyses and sharing of raw data, intermediate analyses, and final results within and across labs. Spyglass uses the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard and includes pipelines for spectral filtering, spike sorting, pose tracking, and neural decoding. Spyglass can be extended to apply existing and newly developed pipelines to datasets from multiple sources. We demonstrate these features in the context of a cross-laboratory replication by applying advanced state space decoding algorithms to publicly available data. New users can try out Spyglass on a Jupyter Hub hosted by HHMI and 2i2c: https://spyglass.hhmi.2i2c.cloud/.

title: AKT is necessary for neuronal hypertrophy and epilepsy caused by Pten knockout.
abstract: Phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is a key negative regulator of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Mutations in PTEN are highly implicated in autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, congenital hydrocephaly and macrocephaly. While the conditional genetic knockout of Pten in murine neurons results in hypertrophy, increased migration, excitatory synaptogenesis, hyperexcitability and epileptiform activity, the specific downstream signalling mediators of these pathologies remain to be fully elucidated. Using retroviral-mediated genetic manipulation of individual neurons within the Cre-lox recombination system, we have analysed pathway outputs in response to the manipulation of various genes using immunohistochemistry, confocal microscopy and extensive morphological analyses, alongside whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology and 120-h video-EEG monitoring for seizure assessment. Here, we demonstrate that signalling through AKT is necessary for the development of neuronal overgrowth, increased excitatory synapse formation, excessive migration and hyperexcitability fuelled by the loss of PTEN function. Notably, the concurrent deletion of Akt1 and Akt3 isoforms was sufficient to effectively rescue hypertrophic neuronal morphology and physiology. These findings establish AKT as the essential mediator through which PTEN deficiency manifests, providing a transformative therapeutic target to correct the morphological and functional defects central to PTEN-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Adoptive T-cell therapies in neuroinfectious and neuroinflammatory diseases.
abstract: Immune dysfunction, spanning pathogenic autoimmunity and impaired host defence, represents a convergent mechanism across neurological autoimmune and inflammatory diseases and opportunistic infections. Despite advances in immunomodulatory and anti-infective therapies, many patients remain treatment-refractory, reflecting limitations of conventional agents. Adoptive T cell therapies introduce dynamic 'living drugs' capable of in vivo expansion, adaptation and persistence. These promising characteristics have led to a rapid proliferation of preliminary reports and clinical trials in inflammatory and infectious diseases of the nervous system, placing neurologists at the forefront of this evolving therapeutic landscape. In this Update, we advance a disease-centred conceptual framework designed to reposition T cell-based therapies within neurological practice. Rather than adopting a technology-driven perspective, we organize disorders according to major patterns of immune dysfunction. Immune deficiency predisposing to opportunistic infection and immune dysregulation driving autoimmunity constitute the principal axes of neurological immune pathology. Within the autoimmune spectrum, distinct immunopathological archetypes (autoantibody-mediated, mixed B and T cell-driven, and disorders at the interface of inflammation and neurodegeneration) provide a pragmatic structure for therapeutic reasoning. Building on this classification, we delineate how adoptive T cells (chimeric antigen receptor T cells, virus-specific T cells and regulatory T cells) may be differentially aligned with underlying disease biology, linking mechanistic insight to clinical strategy.

title: Behavioural rigidity as a transdiagnostic marker of nucleus accumbens dysfunction in dementia.
abstract: Behavioural rigidity, the tendency to persist with inflexible patterns of thoughts or actions, is increasingly recognized as a transdiagnostic symptom across psychiatric, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. Empirical studies exploring the prevalence and underlying neural mechanisms of behavioural rigidity in dementia, however, are lacking. This cross-sectional study sought to delineate the structural and functional neural correlates of behavioural rigidity using a transdiagnostic approach looking across the frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) spectrum and Alzheimer's disease (AD). A total of 204 participants were recruited, including 110 frontotemporal dementia (FTD), 53 AD and 41 healthy older control participants. Within the FTD group, 66 cases were diagnosed with clinically probable behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD), 26 presented with semantic dementia (SD) and 18 cases had progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA). Behavioural rigidity was assessed using the Stereotypical and Motor Behaviour subscale of the Cambridge Behavioural Inventory-Revised. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify grey matter regions associated with behavioural rigidity transdiagnostically, the results of which informed subsequent seed-based voxel-wise functional connectivity analyses. All imaging analyses were adjusted for relevant demographic and technical covariates. Statistical thresholds were set at voxel-level P < 0.001 (uncorrected) and cluster-level P < 0.05 (false discovery rate corrected). Our main finding was that behavioural rigidity is pervasive across dementia subtypes, ranging from most pronounced in bvFTD to milder/relatively absent in PNFA, relative to controls. Whole-brain VBM across the entire patient sample revealed a significant negative association between behavioural rigidity and grey matter intensity exclusively in the bilateral nucleus accumbens. Using the bilateral nucleus accumbens as seeds, resting-state functional connectivity analysis showed that higher levels of behavioural rigidity were associated with stronger connectivity between the left nucleus accumbens and the left supplementary motor area, paracentral lobule and precuneus. This is the first study, to our knowledge, to examine the neural substrates of behavioural rigidity across FTLD syndromes transdiagnostically using structural and functional neuroimaging approaches. Our findings reveal a gradation of rigid and repetitive behaviours, most apparent in bvFTD, which in turn reflects pathological disruption of the nucleus accumbens. Taken together, our findings highlight the need to consider repetitive and rigid behaviours as a transdiagnostic feature in neurodegenerative disorders, and one which indexes underlying nucleus accumbens pathology. More broadly, this study underscores the importance of screening for rigid and repetitive behaviours in the clinic and identifies the nucleus accumbens as a promising neural target to ameliorate these symptoms.

title: Blunted response of caudal locus coeruleus to arousing stimuli in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) causes progressive degeneration of noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC), contributing to non-motor symptoms. Using neuromelanin-sensitive ultra-high field (7 T) MRI, we previously identified a reduction in neuromelanin signal in the caudal LC, indicating a rostro-caudal gradient of noradrenergic cell loss. Caudal LC degeneration was associated with greater severity of non-motor symptoms such as orthostatic hypotension and apathy. In the current case-control study, we expanded the PD cohort to further corroborate the structure-symptom relationships within the LC and investigate how degeneration along the rostro-caudal LC axis affects arousal-related functional responsivity. To this end, 71 people with PD in the ON-medication state and 40 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and 7 T magnetization transfer-weighted (MTw) MRI to quantify structural changes along the rostro-caudal LC axis. A subgroup of 30 people with PD and 27 controls underwent 7 T functional MRI to assess LC responsivity to arousing auditory and visual stimuli in two functional MRI sessions on separate days. Healthy controls were scanned twice without medication, while people with PD were studied on and off dopaminergic medication in counterbalanced order. In the PD group, MTw MRI confirmed a significant reduction of the regional neuromelanin signal in the caudal LC relative to the control group (P = 0.010). This structural disintegration correlated with orthostatic hypotension (P = 0.009) and cognitive impairment (P = 0.036), corroborating its clinical relevance. Functional MRI revealed reduced activation of the caudal LC to arousing visual and auditory stimuli in people with PD relative to controls (P = 0.012). This difference reached statistical significance only in the ON-medication state, with a similar but non-significant trend in the OFF-medication state (P = 0.105). In an exploratory analysis of a smaller subsample, structural and functional caudal LC signals were significantly correlated in both people with PD and healthy controls (P = 0.007). Together, the findings provide evidence for a rostro-caudal gradient of LC pathology in PD at both structural and functional levels. While structural MRI provides fine-grained insights into spatial gradients of disease-related pathology, functional MRI captures the impaired functional responsivity of the caudal LC. The presence of arousal-induced hypoactivation of the caudal LC in the ON-medication state indicates that LC dysfunction extends beyond dopamine deficits in PD, highlighting complex interactions between dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems.

title: Cell-specific transcription dysregulation in human Huntington's disease-positive developing striatum.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG-repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Progressive loss of striatal projection neurons leads to cognitive, psychiatric, and motor impairments that typically manifest in midlife, despite the expansion being present from conception. Increasing evidence supports a neurodevelopmental component to HD; however, authentic human developing HD-positive striatal tissue has not previously been characterised. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to compare an HD-positive human fetal striatal sample to an age- and sex-matched control, with CAG-repeat lengths of 16, 49 and 16, 17 respectively. We also compared the fetal HD-positive transcriptional signature with publicly available datasets from postmortem adult HD-positive brain tissue. We identified 2,032 differentially expressed genes and defined nine cellular clusters.. Gene enrichment analysis revealed alteration of key biological processes across the developing HD-positive striatum, with pathway-level dysregulation varying between clusters. There was substantial overlap in gene expression changes between fetal and adult HD-positive striatal tissues, although not in all transcriptional profiles, and some were reversed. Together, these findings demonstrate that molecular features of HD pathology are present during early human striatal development, supporting the concept that disease mechanisms are established decades prior to clinical onset.

title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a CHCHD10 R15L family.
abstract: Familial forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are potential candidates for gene-directed therapies, but many recently identified genes remain poorly characterized. Here, we provide a comprehensive clinical, neuropathological and biochemical description of familial ALS (fALS) caused by the heterozygous p.R15L missense mutation in the gene CHCHD10. Using a cross-sectional study design, we evaluated five affected and nine unaffected individuals from a large seven-generation pedigree with at least 68 affected members. The pedigree suggests a high (68%-81%) but incomplete disease penetrance. Through cloning of the disease allele from distant members of the family, we establish the disease haplotype in the family. Notably, the haplotype was distinct from that of a previously reported p.R15L mutation carrier with ALS, demonstrating that the variant is in a mutational hotspot. The clinical presentation was notable for being highly stereotyped; all affected individuals presented with the rare ALS variant flail arm syndrome (FAS; also known as brachial amyotrophic diplegia or Vulpian-Bernhardt syndrome), suggesting greater involvement of the cervical spinal cord. Consistently, neuropathology from one family member demonstrated substantially increased CHCHD10 protein aggregation and neuronal loss (though absent TDP-43 pathology) in the cervical versus lumbar spinal cord. This FAS phenotype could be captured by a simple timed finger-tapping task, suggesting potential utility for this task as a clinical biomarker. Additionally, through analysis of fibroblast lines from 12 mutation carriers, isogenic induced pluripotent stem cells and a knock-in mouse model, we determined that CHCHD10 with the R15L variant is stably expressed and retains substantial function both in cultured cells and in vivo, in contrast to prior reports. Conversely, we find loss-of-function (LoF) variants are more common in the population but are not associated with a highly penetrant form of ALS in the UK Biobank (31 in controls; 0 in cases). Together, this argues against LoF and in favour of toxic gain-of-function as the mechanism of disease pathogenesis, similar to the myopathy-causing variants in CHCHD10 (p.G58R and p.S59L). Finally, through proteomic analysis of CSF of variant carriers, we identify that CHCHD10 protein levels are elevated approximately 4-fold in mutation carriers, and that affected and unaffected individuals are differentiated by elevation of two neurofilaments: neurofilament light chain (NfL) and peripherin (PRPH). Collectively, our findings help set the stage for gene-directed therapy for a devasting form of fALS, by establishing the likely disease mechanism and identifying clinical and fluid biomarkers for target engagement and treatment response.

title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Diagnosing multiple sclerosis: implementation and unintended effects of the 2024 McDonald criteria.
abstract: Diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis have evolved substantially since the Schumacher criteria were published in 1965. The most recent iteration, the 2024 McDonald diagnostic criteria, was recently released. Each revision has broadened the range of evidence that can support diagnosis while attempting to preserve specificity. The central question raised by the 2024 revision is therefore not simply whether the criteria are valid in principle, but whether they can be applied safely outside expert centres, where imaging quality, laboratory infrastructure and subspecialist interpretation vary substantially. In this review, we evaluate the 2024 criteria not only as a consensus document but as an intervention in clinical behaviour, with particular attention to misdiagnosis risk, operational feasibility and equity of implementation. In particular, we consider the role of the optic nerve and of the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions in diagnosis, and how the criteria bring more diverse populations and presentations into consideration. We also review how the greater options available to achieve a diagnosis may introduce heterogeneity into diagnostic approaches, and what safeguards can be taken to minimize the risk of inappropriate application of the criteria and subsequent misdiagnosis (and inappropriate treatment). The review finishes by proposing how the changes introduced in this iteration might be refined, with more robust definitions on acquiring and interpreting the novel biomarkers.

title: Divergent tau pathology profiles induced by distinct alpha-synuclein aggregates in non-human primates.
abstract: Proteinopathies are frequently accompanied by co-pathologies, which complicate understanding the pathophysiological mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases. In this study, we employed a well-characterized baboon cohort to investigate the occurrence of tau pathology following intrastriatal injections of two distinct α-synuclein extracts [small aggregates (SA) and large aggregates (LA)] derived from the brains of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). Biochemical and histopathological analyses (6, 12 or 24 months after injections) revealed significantly higher phosphorylated tau expression and greater frequency of neuropil threads in both LA- (n = 18) and SA-injected baboons (n = 12) compared with control animals. We also observed distinct patterns of tau pathology depending on the assembly of α-synuclein aggregates. Baboons injected with SA exhibited tangle-like phosphorylated tau lesions and neuropil threads, with no significant differences across post-injection time points. Moreover, a uniform distribution of tau pathology was detected along the rostro-caudal axis of the medial temporal lobe, affecting neuronal, oligodendroglial and astrocytic cell types. On the other hand, baboons injected with LA exhibited neuropil threads and few glial lesions but lacked phosphorylated tau intraneuronal aggregates. The occurrence of phosphorylated tau lesions was associated with phosphorylated synuclein pathology. These observations suggest a link between nigrostriatal synucleinopathy and limbic tau co-pathology, providing pathophysiological insights into PD dementia.

title: HML-2 env knockdown by AAV9-mediated miRNAs attenuates amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like manifestations in mice.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease, for which there is no cure. Although the precise aetiology of ALS remains elusive, growing evidence suggests a pathogenic role for human endogenous retrovirus-K (HERV-K) in ALS. Expression of HERV-K subtype HML-2 envelope protein in neurons causes neurotoxicity in vitro and induces ALS-like symptoms in mice. We investigated the use of adeno-associated virus-9 (AAV9)-mediated artificial microRNA (amiRNA) targeting the HML-2 env gene in an ALS mouse model. From an in vitro screen of amiRNAs targeting the HML-2 env gene, three were chosen and inserted in tandem into an AAV9 vector and validated in vitro. This approach provided robust silencing of the transgene, with tandem amiRNA achieving robust reduction in gene and protein expression levels. Its therapeutic effectiveness was tested in an HML-2 Env transgenic mouse model, in which the env gene is expressed under the neuron-specific thy1 promoter and develops an ALS-like phenotype. A single intracerebroventricular injection of AAV9 vector encoding the amiRNAs into the mice at postnatal Day 1 effectively reduced HML-2 Env expression in the brain and spinal cord at 84 days post-injection, which was the latest time point studied. Knockdown of HML-2 env decreased the loss of cortical and spinal motor neurons and alleviated muscle fibre degeneration and fibre-type grouping. This led to improved motor function. Our results provide compelling evidence supporting the use of multiple amiRNAs delivered in an AAV9 vector for treating forms of ALS linked to HML-2.

title: Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) is an established treatment for patients with drug-refractory epilepsy, yet long-term therapeutic outcomes are highly variable and challenging to predict. This variability is compounded by the delayed and gradual effects of DBS, the difficulty of consistent seizure monitoring, and the absence of physiological biomarkers to inform treatment. In this study, we analysed longitudinal intracranial recordings over an observational period of 4 years from a cohort of 22 patients with ANT DBS. Our primary goal is the identification of neurophysiological signatures that could predict and track clinical DBS response. Our results show that DBS responders and non-responders exhibit distinct ANT spectral trajectories over time, with responders showing a progressive increase in higher frequencies (β1 and γ) and decreased lower-frequency (δ and θ) activity in comparison to non-responders. Notably, these dynamic biomarkers, particularly high- to low-frequency ratios (e.g. β1/θ), enabled the early discrimination of clinical outcomes. Additionally, we provide evidence of robust circadian and multidien rhythms in ANT local field potentials, with further analyses supporting the feasibility of adaptive stimulation protocols to improve therapeutic outcomes. Together, these findings propose ANT spectral dynamics in outpatient settings as a promising tool for early prediction of therapeutic efficacy and pave the way for biomarker-guided optimization of DBS therapy in epilepsy.

title: Plasma tau-species-positive neuron-derived extracellular vesicles in progressive supranuclear palsy.
abstract: The diagnosis of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) remains challenging, particularly in differentiating it from Parkinson's disease (PD) at early stages. Circulating neuron-derived extracellular vesicles (NDEVs), providing a peripheral window into CNS pathology, might serve as promising biomarkers. A total of 188 participants were recruited from three centres. A discovery cohort [40 PSP patients, 36 PD patients and 31 healthy controls (HCs)] and a multicentre validation cohort (30 PSP patients, 27 PD patients and 24 HCs) were established. NDEVs containing total tau, 4R tau or phosphorylated tau (ptau181, ptau217, ptau231 and ptau396) in plasma samples were analysed using nano-scale flow cytometry. Multivariable logistic regression models were developed in the discovery cohort and strictly validated in the independent cohort using fixed model parameters. In the discovery cohort, the concentrations of tau-, 4R tau-, ptau181- and ptau217-containing NDEVs in PSP patients were significantly higher than those in HCs and PD patients, whereas ptau396-containing NDEVs showed elevation exclusively in PSP compared with HCs (PSP versus HCs: P < 0.001 for tau, P < 0.001 for 4R tau, P < 0.001 for ptau181, P = 0.008 for ptau217, and P = 0.009 for ptau396; PSP versus PD: P < 0.001 for tau, P < 0.001for4R tau, P = 0.029 for ptau181, and P = 0.003 for ptau217). An integrated model incorporating these biomarkers achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.965 (90.0% sensitivity, 96.8% specificity) for distinguishing PSP from HCs and an AUC of 0.963 (87.5% sensitivity, 94.4% specificity) for distinguishing PSP from PD. In the validation cohort, the concentrations of tau-, 4R tau-, ptau181-, ptau217- and ptau396-containing NDEVs in plasma were significantly higher in PSP patients compared with HCs (PSP versus HCs: P < 0.001 for tau, 4R tau and ptau217, P = 0.03 for ptau181, and P = 0.017 for ptau396). Likewise, the concentrations of tau-, 4R tau-, ptau181- and ptau217- were higher in PSP patients than in PD patients (PSP versus PD: P < 0.001 for tau, 4R tau and ptau217, and P = 0.025 for ptau181). The integrated model yielded an AUC of 0.971 for distinguishing PSP from HCs and 0.990 for distinguishing PSP from PD. Notably, in early-stage patients, the integrated model achieved an AUC of 0.987 in differentiating early-stage PSP from PD. These findings indicate that plasma tau-species-containing NDEVs are promising biomarkers for PSP, offering high sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing PSP from both HCs and PD, particularly in early disease stages. Further large-scale, longitudinal studies are warranted to validate these findings fully and explore their role in PSP pathophysiology and progression.

title: Quantitative pathology and APOE genotype reveal dementia risk and progression in Lewy body disease.
abstract: Dementia in Lewy body diseases (LBD) is common and arises through heterogeneous and incompletely understood pathways. Evidence suggests contributions from genetic factors, including APOE ɛ4 genotype, and co-pathology, including concomitant Alzheimer's disease pathology and hypoperfusion related to orthostatic hypotension. However, the relative impact of these factors remains unclear. To address this, we analysed 399 post-mortem brains from LBD cases comprising Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies, and controls, integrating APOE genotype, clinical data and assessment of ischaemic pathology alongside large-scale digital pathology quantification. We established an image analysis pipeline using machine learning to enable automated, standardized measurement of α-synuclein, amyloid-β and phosphorylated tau burden across multiple brain regions. Quantitative pathology was strongly correlated with semi-quantitative ratings and outperformed conventional staging in predicting dementia. Across multiple analytical approaches, APOE ɛ3 and ɛ4 carriers showed distinct dementia risk profiles. APOE ɛ3 carriers developed dementia at lower quantitative α-synuclein and amyloid-β thresholds than ɛ4 carriers, although overall dementia risk was dominated by ɛ4 genotype, consistent with ɛ4 both promoting greater pathology accumulation and modifying the threshold for dementia onset. Orthostatic hypotension and ischaemic pathology increased dementia risk only in ɛ3 carriers with low Lewy and Alzheimer's proteinopathy burden, and male sex further modulated dementia risk for this subgroup. The Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) algorithm identified four trajectories of Lewy pathology progression. Two corresponded to recognized patterns: (i) brainstem first; and (ii) with early amygdala and concomitant brainstem involvement. Two further patterns showed early cortical involvement: (i) with early cingulate cortex involvement together with brainstem pathology; and (ii) starting in the neocortex before limbic and brainstem involvement. Co-pathology progression modelling identified subtypes with early predominance of amyloid-β, phosphorylated tau or α-synuclein and showed that Lewy subtypes follow two propagation trajectories in opposite directions. Together, these findings demonstrate that integrating quantitative pathology with genotype and clinical data reveals distinct yet overlapping pathways to dementia in LBD, refining disease progression models and providing a basis for genotype- and pathology-informed patient stratification in therapeutic trials.
