title: Pathology in resected areas of FDG PET hypometabolism in pediatric epilepsy patients with focal cortical dysplasia type II
abstract: Introduction: [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) frequently reveals hypometabolism extending beyond MRI-visible focal cortical dysplasia (FCD). Whether surrounding hypometabolic areas harbour pathological cells remains unclear. We compared histopathology between the lesion epicentre and surrounding hypometabolic borders in children undergoing epilepsy surgery. Methods: Fourteen children with intractable, extra-temporal focal epilepsy (mean age 9.0{+/-}5.0 years; 9 female) were retrospectively reviewed. Resections encompassed the visually-apparent MRI signal abnormalities as well as areas of surrounding FDG-PET hypometabolism when safely feasible. Multiple pathological specimens were obtained from the epicentre and surrounding hypometabolic areas. Overall, 136 specimens were analyzed: 64 epicentre (median 4{+/-}3/patient) and 72 border (median 5{+/-}4/patient). Results: Pathology was identified in 75% of epicentre specimens (59% with frank FCD (fFCD) IIa/b, 16% with dysmorphic neurons only (DNO)). Border specimens showed pathology in 62% (31% fFCD IIa/b, 31% DNO). We fitted a Bayesian logistic mixed model with pathology as outcome variable, location as predictor, and subject as a random effect. Compared to negative pathology, the log-odds of fFCD in the epicentre was 1.00 (credible interval (CI) 0.32, 1.77) and -1.25 in the border (CI -2.17, -0.40). The log-odds of DNO vs negative pathology was non-significant in both locations. Exploratory analyses did not show significant associations between pathology and degree of regional hypometabolism or volume. All patients achieved Engel Ia status at one-year follow-up with no long-term neurological deficits. Conclusion: These findings suggest a spatial difference in distribution of histopathology, with fFCD concentrated in the epicentre and DNO present in both the epicentre and hypometabolic borders. Thus, FDG-PET may be used to better detect the histopathological borders of FCD type II, and the high seizure-freedom rate presented here supports the inclusion of these surrounding hypometabolic regions in the surgical resection (when safe to do so), improving the likelihood of removing potentially epileptogenic cells.

title: Sex differences in cell type-specific transcriptional programs and GPCR signaling in the human subgenual anterior cingulate cortex
abstract: Psychiatric conditions show marked sex differences in disease onset, symptom presentation, and response to treatments. Understanding how sex differences manifest across molecularly distinct neuronal populations in individuals without psychiatric conditions may help explain sex-dependent variation in neural circuit function and treatment response. Here, we examined molecularly distinct cell types within the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) of non-psychiatric subjects. Using RNA sequencing data previously generated from laser-capture microdissected neurons, we investigated sex differences in gene expression and co-expression networks in excitatory pyramidal neurons (layers 2/3 and 5/6) and somatostatin (SST)-, parvalbumin (PVALB)-, and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing inhibitory interneurons (N=10 males, 9 females). We identified sex differences in transcriptomic profiles, biological pathways, and co-expression network connectivity. PVALB cells showed stronger overall female transcriptional enrichment, while SST cells exhibited male-enriched transcriptional signatures. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified PVALB and SST modules more connected in males and females, respectively, which included hub genes involved in immune, extracellular matrix, and bioenergetic processes. Since G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are viable therapeutic targets, we examined sex differences in GPCR transcripts. Across all GPCR-cell-type combinations, CHRM2 in PVALB cells showed the second strongest sex difference (enriched in females). To test the functional relevance of this difference, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology in mouse prefrontal cortex. M2 receptor activation increased maximal firing rates in PVALB cells from female but not male mice. Collectively, our findings demonstrate cell type-specific sex differences in the sgACC corresponding to functional differences in neuromodulator signaling, with potential implications for treatment response.

title: Sex-specific gene and isoform expression characterizes hippocampal aging in rhesus macaques
abstract: Aging produces widespread transcriptomic alterations that extend beyond changes in gene expression to include changes at the isoform level. Declining splicing fidelity, including increased intron retention and aberrant isoform expression, has been proposed to contribute to cellular dysfunction; however, the extent and biological significance of isoform-specific changes in the aging brain remain poorly understood. Age-related cognitive decline has also been associated with neuroinflammation and the development of a chronic inflammatory state, or ''inflammaging,'' within the brain. Here, we used short- and long-read RNA sequencing to characterize gene- and isoform-level changes associated with hippocampal aging across sex in 24 rhesus macaques. We identified 594 age-associated differential isoform expression events, comprising both shared and sex-specific changes. Inflammatory pathways, including TNF- -- NF-{kappa}B signaling, interferon responses, and complement pathways, were enriched across both sexes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified sex-specific modules associated with inflammatory, glial, mitochondrial, and hormone-responsive processes. Notably, several age-associated changes were detected at the isoform level despite limited or absent corresponding gene-level differences, highlighting transcript-level regulation as an additional dimension of brain aging that may be overlooked by gene-level analyses. To investigate the relationship between aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD), we independently performed WGCNA on the rhesus macaque cohort and a publicly available human hippocampal AD single-nucleus RNA-sequencing dataset (GSE268609). Cross-species module preservation and gene overlap analyses identified shared genes between age-associated and AD-associated networks, with pathway enrichment implicating glial function, inflammation, and mitochondrial biology. Together, these findings highlight sex-associated differences in hippocampal transcriptomic aging, underscore the importance of isoform-level regulation, and identify shared transcriptional signatures between normal aging and AD-associated pathways.

title: Simple, static, spiking nonlinearities can account for seemingly complex interactions between visual, motor and cognitive variables in the visual cortex.
abstract: Neural activity in the visual cortex is driven by the stimulus and modulated by multiple task-related variables, including spatial attention, eye movements, and perceptual decisions. These multiple influences are each typically described as nonlinear interactions such as gain or normalization, raising the question of how these diverse signals can be combined through cellular or circuit mechanisms. Here we address this problem by examining neuronal responses in macaque visual areas V2 and V3 during a visual discrimination task that dissociates spatial attention from motor planning and microsaccadic eye movements. Using a statistical modeling framework, we show that attentional, microsaccade-related, and choice-related influences on neural activity are best explained by a simple additive stimulus-independent input modulation, which manifests as a gain via a spiking nonlinearity. In addition to explaining how interactions between variables might be accomplished mechanistically, this framework also resolves a controversy about the relationship between microsaccades and spatial attention. We find that neither microsaccade direction nor microsaccade-related neural activity accounts for attentional modulation, although these variables are often correlated, leading to apparent interactions. Thus, visual cortex can integrate sensory, motor-related, and cognitive signals through a parsimonious mechanism that preserves stable stimulus representations while supporting flexible, context-dependent modulation.

title: Social vision expands into auditory cortices of people born deaf: evidence from naturalistic film and encoding models
abstract: Comparing deaf and hearing adults provides insight into the contribution of experience to function of auditory cortical networks. We used naturalistic fMRI and voxel-wise encoding to measure information processing in auditory networks of deaf (n=24) and hearing (n=22) adults who watched a 35-minute silent animated film. Unlike simpler stimuli, naturalistic films are rich in a broad range of perceptual, affective, and social features, including motion, dynamic social interactions, and Theory of Mind. Machine vision algorithms and human coding were used to densely annotate visual and social film features. In both groups we observed a right-lateralized processing hierarchy with encoding of low-level visual features in early visual areas, social visual features along the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and Theory of Mind in temporoparietal junction. In deaf participants, auditory cortices showed enhanced encoding of a broad range of visual information, from low level motion to Theory of Mind. In higher order auditory networks, social interactions emerging as the strongest predictor of neural activity in deaf people and showed the strongest enhancement in deafness. Auditory networks of deaf adults showed systematic anatomical organization within and across hemispheres. Within the right hemisphere, higher-order auditory regions neighboring the STS preferentially responded to social visual features whereas lower-level visual features were represented broadly across the auditory hierarchy. These results suggest that proximity and connectivity principles govern anatomical expansion of information encoding in sensory loss.

title: Task structure flexibly shifts working memory formats across cortical circuits
abstract: Short-term memory in delayed-response tasks is widely attributed to choice-predictive activity in frontal cortex, maintained by discrete attractor dynamics in thalamocortical circuits. Here we ask whether this mechanism extends to tasks where cues specify goals rather than actions. We trained rats on two auditory delayed-response tasks: an egocentric task, where cues mapped to movement directions, and an allocentric task, where cues specified world-centered locations. Using electrophysiology and optogenetics, we found that the egocentric task engaged early sensorimotor transformation and prospective motor planning in secondary motor cortex (M2). The allocentric task, however, relied on a delayed sensorimotor transformation: auditory cortex carried a retrospective sensory trace, whereas M2 neither encoded choice nor was required for its maintenance during the delay. Simplifying the allocentric task to a single start position rapidly reinstated early transformation and M2 dependence within the same animals. These results demonstrate that animals flexibly select the timing of sensorimotor transformation, and that this choice determines the format and cortical locus of working memory.

title: Taste preferences are influenced by temperature and the TRPM8 thermoreceptor
abstract: Oral temperature influences perceptual and behavioral responses to taste stimuli. Whether somatosensory processes contribute to this influence is unknown. Here we studied how stimulus temperature impacted mouse taste preferences and how these preferences were affected by the absence of TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8). TRPM8 is a thermoreceptor supporting cool and warm temperature coding by somatosensory, including lingual trigeminal, neurons. Female and male TRPM8 gene deficient (KO) and C57BL/6J (B6) control mice (n = 69) entered thermolickometry tests that measured licking to two solutions of one taste chemical with different concentration-temperature properties across randomly interleaved brief-access (10-sec long) fluid exposure trials. Tastants were 15{degrees}C and 30{degrees}C bitter quinine (0.03 and 0.3 mM) or an appetitive sugar (sucrose or glucose, 100 and 500 mM). Mice were water-restricted or -replete during quinine and sugar tests, respectively, which were conducted separately and examined all possible concentration-temperature pairings across multiple days. Linear mixed model (LMM) analysis revealed that concentration and temperature both individually and additively affected licks emitted to quinine, with higher concentration and higher temperature (30{degrees}C) associated with the greatest reduction in quinine licks in B6 and KO mice. In contrast, LMM analysis indicated that temperature influenced licks to sugar only in KO mice, which made significantly fewer licks to higher than lower temperature sugars. Notably, KO mice also showed significantly reduced avidity to lick concentrated sugars than B6 mice. These data uncover novel roles for oral temperature and the TRPM8 thermoreceptor, and possibly its broader physiological influences, in taste preference behavior.

title: Temporal Variability in Brain Connectivity for Estimating Two-Year Clinical Severity in Mild Cognitive Impairment
abstract: Resting-state functional MRI measures coordinated activity across brain networks and may reveal early changes relevant to cognitive decline. Conventional  static functional connectivity analyses often compute time-series correlations across an entire scan, missing informative fluctuations over shorter timescales. We investigated whether these fluctuations, in fMRI scans collected at baseline, improve estimation of clinical severity two years later in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). In 48 ADNI participants with MCI, we summarized temporal variability using the standard deviation of windowed correlations between 21 pairs of brain networks. Using repeated nested cross-validation, the mean absolute error in predicting follow-up Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) was 1.62 points with clinical covariates alone, 1.66 after adding static connectivity, and 1.51 after adding connectivity variability. With additional motion covariates, the corresponding errors were 1.70, 1.73, and 1.59. Connectivity variability outperformed both conventional models in all three cross-validation repetitions, while randomized signals preserving the complete cross-spectrum did not reproduce the improvement. Perhaps surprisingly though, most of the gain occurred in participants without subsequent clinical worsening, and results were sensitive to the choice of temporal windows. These preliminary findings suggest that compact measures of connectivity variability may capture clinically relevant information beyond conventional measures of  static functional connectivity, motivating larger studies to evaluate their value for predicting future cognitive impairment.

title: Temporal stability for individual differences in both habit learning and expression
abstract: Actions transition from goal-directed to stimulus-driven habits through repetition. Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume that overreliance on habitual control drives maladaptive behaviors. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 313), we assessed stimulus-response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, with computational modelling further supporting trait-like tendencies for habit learning and expression. Trait-like tendencies were also reflected in action automatization while practicing stimulus-response associations, which was associated with future habitual behavior. Our findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of habit formation and its role in psychopathology.

title: The C. elegans Connectome Toolbox: an open, extensible framework for multimodal connectomic data integration and analysis
abstract: The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions. These datasets now serve as foundational resources that underpin studies into the neuronal basis of C. elegans behavior. In spite of their high utility, heterogeneity in the different datasets and their annotation conventions obscures direct comparison where discrepancies between connectomes frequently stem from differences in coverage or nomenclature rather than genuine biological disagreement. Additionally, datasets describing new connectivity modalities - contact-based (the contactome), extrasynaptic (monoaminergic and neuropeptidergic), and functional connectivity - have also recently become available. Thus, there is a need for a unified framework providing standardized access to these diverse datasets while preserving their individual provenance. Here, we present the C. elegans Connectome Toolbox, a comprehensive framework for consolidating, curating and validating historical and newly published multimodal C. elegans connectivity data. Connectome Toolbox includes an accessible online resource (https://openworm.org/ConnectomeToolbox) for interactive data exploration and is accompanied by a Python library for programmatic access. We demonstrate the utility of the toolbox through a series of analyses that illustrate how connectome data can be explored, visualized, and compared across modalities, including integration of the anatomical connectome with a comprehensive neurotransmitter atlas, and comparison with computational models of C. elegans neural circuits.

title: Traveling waves in attention networks inherit the rhythms of sensory systems
abstract: Attention emerges from coordinated activity across distributed brain regions, each with their own intrinsic rhythm: alpha (7-12Hz) in visual cortex and theta (3-7Hz) in auditory cortex. When attention is sustained on a visual location, alpha power increases over the corresponding ipsilateral hemisphere, a robust neurophysiological marker of sustained visuospatial attention named alpha lateralization. Hemispheric asymmetry during sustained attention was recently also reported for anterior-to-posterior alpha traveling waves -smooth phase shifts across the cortex. This finding suggests that traveling waves support top-down inter-areal communication within the attention network. Here we asked whether traveling waves indeed reflect top-down attention signals or are merely a byproduct of sustained visuospatial attention. We manipulated attention through different sensory modalities (auditory cueing and visual stimulation), thus engaging different sensory cortices, while maintaining the task as visual discrimination. Using electroencephalography, we tested the hypothesis that if traveling waves reflect attention signals within the network, their frequency should follow the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system: theta for auditory cueing and alpha for visual stimulation. If instead they are a byproduct of attention allocated to visual information, their frequency should remain in alpha. Our results support the former: auditory cueing led to lateralized theta traveling waves, while visual stimulation produced lateralized alpha traveling waves. Crucially, traveling-wave lateralization in both frequencies correlated with trial-by-trial alpha power lateralization. Together, attention signals appear to propagate as waves at the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system and locally modulate alpha power lateralization in task-relevant visual regions.

title: Use of Integrative Proteomic Analysis to Uncover Shared Molecular Signatures Across Distinct Forms of Hydrocephalus
abstract: Hydrocephalus is a heterogeneous disease characterized by disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics and can arise from diverse etiologies, including post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH), hydrocephalus following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), post-infectious hydrocephalus (PIH), and idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). Hydrocephalus has high disease burden in pediatric and older populations and a marked increase in prevalence with advancing age. Despite this high incidence, the underpinning molecular and signaling pathway alterations remain incompletely understood. Hence CSF proteomic profiling would enable a robust and high-resolution approach for exploring disease-specific biomarkers and to discover shared molecular mechanisms underlying hydrocephalus. In this study, we performed a cross-study proteomic analysis to evaluate biomarker proteins reported across PHH, SAH, PIH, and iNPH groups. Using published proteomic datasets, we comparatively analyzed CSF proteins to investigate the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), their common molecular signatures, and enriched biological pathways across hydrocephalus groups. Across etiologies, recurrently altered proteins were predominantly associated with inflammatory signaling (cytokine, chemokine, interleukin-(IL-17), tumor necrosis factor (TNF)), toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, blood-brain-barrier (BBB) disruption leading to coagulation cascades, and neuronal injury responses. Hemorrhage-associated forms of hydrocephalus (PHH and SAH) demonstrated enriched coagulation and hemoglobin-related pathways, whereas infection associated forms (PIH) showed enhanced immune and inflammatory responses. iNPH exhibited alterations in proteins linked to neurodegeneration, synaptic function, and impaired CSF clearance. Interestingly, our cross-study analyses identified recurrently dysregulated proteins across hydrocephalus subtypes. Collectively, our cross-study proteomic analyses define shared and etiology-specific proteomic signatures across hydrocephalus subtypes and identify potential CSF-based biomarkers for diagnostic stratification and future precision therapeutic approaches.

title: A novel mechanism for morphological change during bacterial sporulation based on programmed peptidoglycan degradation.
abstract: Many bacteria form spores to endure unfavorable conditions. While Firmicutes generate endospores through cell division, sporulation in non-Firmicutes remains less understood. The Gram-negative bacterium Myxococcus xanthus undergoes sporulation through two distinct mechanisms: rapid sporulation triggered by chemical induction and slow sporulation driven by starvation, both occurring independently of cell division. Instead, these processes depend on the complete degradation of the peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall by two lytic transglycosylases (LTGs), LtgA and LtgB. Remarkably, LtgB programs the pace of PG degradation by LtgA during rapid sporulation, ensuring a controlled process that prevents abrupt PG breakdown and the formation of non-resistant pseudospores. In addition to regulation between LTGs, PG degradation is also influenced by its synthesis; cells exhibiting increased muropeptide production often circumvent sporulation. These findings not only reveal novel mechanisms of bacterial sporulation but also shed light on the regulatory network governing PG dynamics.

title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain.
abstract: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept - in the form of the number zero - has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

title: Dopaminergic neurons linking threat processing to cardiac modulation and locomotor responses.
abstract: Heartbeat and behavior are tightly coordinated during defensive states, yet the neuronal mechanisms linking threat processing to cardiac modulation-and the potential contribution of cardiac dynamics to behavioral output-remain poorly understood. Here, using simultaneous recordings of heartbeat and behavior in tethered Drosophila, we show that mechanical threat triggers locomotion together with rapid cardiac deceleration. We identify two pairs of dopaminergic neurons, termed DA-WED neurons, that mediate this cardiac response. Silencing these neurons markedly attenuates threat-induced cardiac deceleration, whereas optogenetic activation induces cardiac deceleration in the absence of threat. Two-photon calcium imaging further shows that DA-WED neurons are activated by mechanical threat, and manipulating their activity bidirectionally modulates threat-induced locomotion. Linking cardiac dynamics to behavior, direct optogenetic manipulation of cardiomyocytes that quantitatively reproduces threat-evoked cardiac deceleration is accompanied by increased locomotion. Together, these results identify a dopaminergic descending pathway that links threat processing to cardiac modulation and suggest that cardiac dynamics may contribute to shaping defensive behavior.

title: Gcn5 and mTORC1 mediated regulation of autophagy controls Drosophila blood cell homeostasis.
abstract: Blood progenitors are regulated by a variety of systemic and nutritional cues from their environment. In the Drosophila lymph gland (LG), the Posterior Signaling Center acts as a stem cell niche striking a balance between progenitors and differentiated blood cells. Autophagy is a vital cellular process that maintains homeostasis by removing unnecessary or dysfunctional cell components through autophagic degradation and recycling. Here, using genetic perturbation analysis, we show that autophagy plays a critical role in regulating LG blood cell homeostasis. General control non-derepressible 5 (Gcn5), a histone acetyltransferase, is expressed in the primary LG lobe, and modulation of Gcn5 levels perturbs LG homeostasis. Our results show that hemocyte-specific Gcn5 modulation controls autophagic flux in the hemocytes. Furthermore, we show that modulation of mTORC1 activity can perturb hematopoiesis. Our results indicate that organismal Gcn5 levels respond to dietary shifts and are modulated by mTORC1 signaling. Chemical intervention shows that mTORC1 overrides the effect exerted by Gcn5 in regulating LG hematopoiesis. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Gcn5 and mTORC1 regulate autophagy to maintain blood cell homeostasis in Drosophila.

title: Spectraplakin is required for dendritic microtubule organization via a tip-based mechanism in Drosophila.
abstract: The differential microtubule organization in axons and dendrites underlies neuronal polarity and developmental processes, like neurite pruning. How neurons achieve their specific microtubule organization during development is an area of active research, and it has been especially hard to explain how dendritic microtubules are oriented with their plus ends toward the soma. Transient microtubule nucleation from tips of early growing dendrites has been proposed as a mechanism that would explain how this orientation is set up. In a survey for cytoskeletal regulators involved in dendrite pruning and microtubule organization in Drosophila, we found the spectraplakin Short stop (Shot), an actin/microtubule crosslinker. Loss of Shot causes microtubule orientation defects already during early dendrite development, when Shot is transiently recruited to tips of growing dendrites via its actin-binding domain. Genetic and functional evidence suggests that Shot's primary function in this process is to locally stabilize microtubules. We also provide evidence for an independent, developmentally transient microtubule nucleation mechanism. Our data highlight the importance of transient and localized microtubule regulation for dendritic microtubule organization.

title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study.
abstract: Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

title: A genome-wide CRISPR screening identifies targets that drive tolerogenic dendritic cells.
abstract: Tolerogenic dendritic cells (TolDCs) contribute to immune tolerance and have demonstrated therapeutic potential in early clinical studies of autoimmune diseases. However, the key molecular pathways driving their differentiation and tolerogenic phenotype remain elusive. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the functional status of TolDCs in response to different tolerizing agents and identified CD86 as a consistent and robust marker downregulated in tolerogenic state. CD86 is functionally required for TolDC-mediated suppression of T cell proliferation and cytokine secretion, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of tolerogenic potential. Leveraging CD86 expression as a readout, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen and characterized genes associated with TolDC phenotypes. This approach positions UBE2L6 as a regulator of CD86 expression through modulation of an ISG15-USP18-associated pathway, implicating its involvement in tolerogenic functions. These findings describe therapeutically targetable pathways to promote immune tolerance.

title: A pangene family atlas of cereals uncovers hidden intraspecific and interspecific diversity.
abstract: Pangenomes are reshaping gene-family analysis by shifting from single-genome views to pangene families, yet many studies still rely on orthogroups as proxies, overlooking crucial allele- and locus-level diversity. Here, we present a pangene-based and domain-defined framework to construct and analyze nearly 500 pangene families across four major cereals. Compared with single-genome analyses, pangenome-level family membership increases by 59-264%, and many families show pangene accumulation curves that remain far from saturation, indicating that substantial allelic diversity is still uncharacterized even when 320 rice genomes are included. We further quantify family behavior along three complementary dimensions and reveal extensive remodeling of membership and copy-number allocation that is largely invisible when only total family size is considered. Together, this framework and its associated resource provide a foundation for deeper use of plant pangenomes, offering new insight into how evolutionary constraints and diversification shape pangene families.

title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity.
abstract: The lifelong continuity of neuronal function rests upon the perdurance of neurons, synapses and neural circuits that are sustained, in part, by homeostatic signaling. Currently, the implementation of homeostatic signaling within complex brain circuitry remains poorly defined. Given the tremendous diversity of cell and synapse types, is homeostatic plasticity deployed in a cell-type specific manner and, if so, what are the rules? Here, we report that presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is achieved in a target neuron-specific manner. PHP is robust at synapses that contact parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and absent at somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons. Furthermore, PHP can be differentially induced at adjacent synapses that are present within single axonal boutons, separated by hundreds of nanometers. These highly localized effects are eliminated in the absence of Sema3A signaling, a homeostatic signaling molecule. Our data suggest a model where PHP is repressed throughout axons that contact SST+ interneurons and locally de-repressed with nanoscale precision.

title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists.
abstract: Circadian physiology coordinates systemic and cellular metabolism through a light-entrained central clock and metabolically synchronized peripheral clocks. Whether feeding-fasting cycles or tumor-intrinsic clocks primarily set tumor metabolic state is unclear. Here, we profiled colorectal cancer (CRC) responses to PPAR antagonists across 2D and 3D CRC models and tumor-bearing mice. In standard high-glucose, low-fat medium, Bmal1 oscillations and daily variation in PPAR antagonist sensitivity were apparent in CRC cells. By contrast, nutrient-defined media that recapitulate feeding and nighttime fasting abolished time-dependent variability and unified drug responses across models. Still, the fed state selectively sensitized spheroids and patient-derived organoids to PPAR-γ antagonism. In mice, dosing PPAR-γ antagonist in the fed state prolonged survival and reduced hepatotoxicity. The use of Bmal-1-silenced CRC cells validated that feeding-fasting rhythms, not tumor-intrinsic clocks, govern CRC sensitivity to PPAR antagonists. Our study also supports the predictive capacity of nutrient-alternating 3D tumor models, enabling metabolism-targeted anticancer treatment evaluation.

title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses.
abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines require annual reformulation due to antigenic drift and provide suboptimal protection. Here, we evaluate self-amplifying mRNA (samRNA) vaccines encoding chimeric (cHA) and mosaic (mHA) hemagglutinins representing influenza A virus HA phylogenetic groups 1 and 2. Following prime-boost immunization, group 1 cHA vaccines (cH8/1-cH5/1) elicit broad cross-reactive antibodies and confer complete protection against diverse H1N1 strains covering decades of antigenic drift. Group 2 vaccines (cH4/3-cH15/3 and mH10/3-mH14/3) provide comparable breadth against multiple H3N2 strains and heterosubtypic H7N9 challenge, with cHA samRNA showing superior cross-group protection. Protection is associated with Fc-mediated effector functions and CD4+ T cell responses, with minimal hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing titers. Passive serum transfer confirms antibody-mediated protection independent of cellular immunity. Protective immunity is maintained at doses as low as 0.4 μg, demonstrating the dose-sparing advantage of the samRNA platform. These results support samRNA-delivered cHA and mHA antigens as promising candidates for broadly protective influenza vaccines.

title: Succinate promotes multiple myeloma cell proliferation through TCA cycle oxidation.
abstract: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy that develops within the bone marrow. The bone marrow metabolome is altered in myeloma, with implications for malignant cell growth. Here, the impact of elevated bone marrow levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite, succinate, was interrogated. Succinate was found to promote proliferation of several myeloma cell lines. This was linked to its uptake and oxidation in the TCA cycle, as indicated by increased ATP-coupled mitochondrial respiration and incorporation of succinate-derived carbons into downstream TCA cycle intermediates, which also occurs in primary myeloma cells. Succinate-driven proliferation was dependent upon mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and abrogated by ATP synthase inhibition. Furthermore, interrogation of large-scale transcriptomic data identified that elevated expression of a mitochondrial succinate transporter associates with accelerated disease progression in myeloma, indicating this mechanism may promote plasma cell growth in vivo and highlighting a target for therapeutic intervention.

title: TNF- and IL-1-induced inflammation are enhanced through cooperative interactions between Nrf2 and NF-κB.
abstract: Reactive oxygen species are typically elevated at inflammatory sites due to influx of large numbers of neutrophils and other myeloid cells that produce oxygen free radicals as microbicidal agents. However, although oxidative stress is frequently implicated as an initiator or amplifier of inflammation, particularly in the context of cancer, the key mediators of reactive oxygen-driven inflammation require clarification. Here we show that the redox-responsive transcription factor, Nrf2, can act as an enhancer of TNF- and IL-1-initiated inflammation. Silencing or deletion of the Nrf2 antagonist, Keap1, led to robustly enhanced TNF- or IL-1-driven inflammatory cytokine production. Conversely, suppression of Nrf2 activation blunted inflammation in the same contexts. Mechanistically, Nrf2 enhanced inflammation through cooperative interactions with p65 RelA at NFκB-regulated promoters. These observations reveal a direct link between the Keap1/Nrf2 reactive oxygen-sensing pathway and TNF- or IL-1-initiated inflammation and suggest that Nrf2 can act as a rheostat for NFκB-dependent inflammatory outputs.

title: Terminus est: Repurposing public RNA-seq data to map 3' transcript termini in bacteria.
abstract: Bar and colleagues1 repurpose publicly available RNA sequencing data to identify 3' transcript termini across a diverse collection of bacteria. This presents a major resource for investigating transcript termination and processing, with initial investigations into the diversity and conservation of termini.

title: Directional evolution of parasitoid strategies and contingent host shifts shape the radiation of Darwin wasps (Ichneumonidae).
abstract: Evolutionary change is not always reversible: some traits evolve repeatedly in one direction but rarely in the other, forming evolutionary "ratchets" that constrain future trajectories. Parasitoid wasps provide a powerful system to test this idea because their modes of host exploitation range from relatively simple strategies to highly integrated developmental interactions with living hosts. Here, we investigate the evolution of parasitoid strategies and host use across Darwin wasps (Ichneumonidae), the most diverse parasitoid family, using a phylogenomic dataset comprising 697 species and all ichneumonid subfamilies. Our results reveal that the evolution of parasitoid strategies is strikingly asymmetric: transitions from idiobiosis (permanent host paralysis) to koinobiosis (in which hosts continue development after oviposition) and from ectoparasitoidism to endoparasitoidism occurred repeatedly, whereas reversals were virtually absent. In contrast, host associations were dynamic but contingent on parasitoid strategy: moths and butterflies (Lepidoptera) were inferred as the ancestral hosts, but repeated host shifts subsequently occurred across nearly all holometabolous insect orders despite strong phylogenetic conservatism within major lineages. However, this flexibility was strongly asymmetric, with host-taxon shifts occurring predominantly in idiobiont lineages and becoming much rarer after transitions to koinobiosis. These results show that macroevolutionary dynamics can differ sharply among interacting traits, with directional evolutionary ratchets reshaping not only individual trait trajectories but also the ecological options available to diversifying lineages.

title: Sleep-like slow waves in wakefulness index post-stroke behavioural alterations.
abstract: Increases in high-amplitude, low-frequency EEG oscillations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep serve as markers of neuronal silencing, which disrupts functional connectivity and is associated with a loss of awareness and responsiveness. Cortical slowing likewise occurs during wakefulness, upon sleep deprivation, and accompanies performance deterioration. Recent work has revealed similar oscillations (termed 'sleep-like slow waves') following stroke in brain regions close or connected to a brain lesion, offering a plausible but untested mechanism for stroke-related behavioural impairment. Here, we simultaneously recorded EEG and behavioural performance while 30 unilateral stroke patients (12 left hemisphere, 18 right hemisphere) and 27 age-matched healthy adults completed a computerised perceptual decision-making task. Stroke patients had predominantly middle cerebral artery strokes (n=25), with a small subset of posterior cerebral artery (n=4), and anterior cerebral artery/middle cerebral artery (n=1) lesions. Sleep-like slow waves occurred more frequently in stroke patients relative to healthy controls, with limited spatial specificity when comparing patients with left and right lesion sites (more slow waves ipsilateral of the lesion). Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between slow wave occurrence and the accuracy and speed of perceptual reports in stroke patients, suggesting that variations in the occurrence of slow waves may contribute to cognitive heterogeneity post-stroke. As sleep-like slow waves predict deficits in perceptual decision-making following stroke, they represent a plausible mechanism of post-lesion functional network dysfunction extending beyond the damaged regions, thereby contributing to broader cognitive impairments.

title: A spectral partial information decomposition framework for quantifying information about cognitive variables in oscillatory brain networks.
abstract: Neural oscillations are thought to play a central role in encoding and transmitting cognitive information across large-scale brain networks, yet the relative contributions of phase synchrony and amplitude co-modulations to distributed coding remain unclear. A key obstacle is the absence of tools that can simultaneously quantify task-relevant information in the frequency domain and disentangle its phase and amplitude co-modulation components across pairwise and higher order interactions. Here, we introduce a spectral partial information decomposition framework (NeOPID) for quantifying information about cognitive variables in amplitude co-modulation and phase contributions, and to quantify redundant and synergistic information in brain relations, from pairwise to higher-order interactions. We validated the approach on Kuramoto and Stuart- Landau oscillator networks, including a whole-brain model constrained by macaque anatomical connectivity. NeOPID accurately recovers ground-truth encoding schemes and reveals that phase relations and amplitude co-modulations act as complementary coding channels with both redundant and synergistic components. NeOPID further extends this decomposition to higher-order functional interactions enabling the characterization of how cognitive information is collectively distributed across multiple oscillatory edges via redundant and synergistic encoding. To illustrate biological applicability, we applied NeOPID to local field potentials (LFPs) recorded from the macaque fronto-parietal network during a working memory task. In this dataset, NeOPID identified beta-band amplitude co-modulations as the primary carrier of stimulus information, and revealed that higher-order phase interactions exhibit both redundant and synergistic structure during the memory delay. These results establish NeOPID as a principled tool for dissecting the informational architecture about cognitive processes of oscillatory brain networks.Significance Statement Understanding how the brain coordinates large-scale communication to support cognition remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Characterizing the distinct roles of phase synchrony and amplitude co-modulation has been hindered by a lack of computational approaches capable of separating these components across pairwise and higher-order interactions. Here, we introduce NeOPID (neural spectral Partial Information Decomposition), a framework designed to isolate phase and amplitude co-modulation contributions and quantify redundant and synergistic information contained in pair-wise and higher order functional interactions. NeOPID was validated on simulated oscillator models and on macaque local field potentials (LFPs) during a working memory task. Overall, the results establish NeOPID as a principled tool for dissecting the informational architecture underlying cognitive processes in oscillatory brain networks.

title: AgRP neurons as an integrative node linking the somatotropic and reproductive axes.
abstract: Growth hormone (GH) signaling contributes to pubertal development and reproductive function, yet the hypothalamic circuits mediating these effects remain incompletely understood. Kisspeptin and agouti-related protein (AgRP) neurons are key integrators of metabolic and reproductive cues and exhibit GH-responsive signaling pathways. We therefore investigated their contributions to the reproductive consequences of altered somatotropic signaling. Using genetic mouse models of chronic GH excess or deficiency, we examined the impact of altered GH signaling on pubertal maturation, fertility, and hypothalamic neuroendocrine function. Pubertal onset was unaffected in female mice, whereas males with either GH excess or GH deficiency exhibited delayed puberty. In contrast, GH hypersecretion selectively disrupted estrous cyclicity and impaired fertility in females. Female reproductive dysfunction occurred despite preserved kisspeptin signaling, as evidenced by the preservation of intrinsic electrophysiological properties of kisspeptin neurons and unaltered hypothalamic Kiss1 mRNA expression. Chronic GH excess increased hypothalamic Agrp mRNA expression and reduced Pomc and Tac2 mRNA expression compared to control mice; these transcriptional changes were prevented by AgRP-specific GH receptor (GHR) deletion, which also improved ovarian function. Notably, selective deletion of the GHR in AgRP cells markedly improved fertility in GH-hypersecreting females. Together, these findings identify AgRP neurons as a critical hypothalamic target through which chronic GH excess impairs female reproductive function. Our results further demonstrate that GH-induced infertility occurs independently of canonical kisspeptin-GnRH dysfunction, revealing a sexually dimorphic mechanism linking somatotropic signaling to reproductive competence.Significance Statement Reproductive dysfunction is a common consequence of chronic alterations in growth hormone (GH) secretion, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly defined. We show that chronic GH excess induces a sexually dimorphic reproductive phenotype characterized by profound impairment of female fertility despite largely preserved kisspeptin neuronal function. In contrast, GH excess altered hypothalamic AgRP-associated pathways, and the selective deletion of GH receptors in AgRP neurons significantly improved fertility in GH-hypersecreting females. These findings identify AgRP neurons as key mediators of GH-induced reproductive dysfunction and reveal a previously unrecognized sexually dimorphic neuroendocrine mechanism linking somatotropic signaling, metabolic circuits, and female fertility.

title: Cell-type- and subregion-specific basolateral amygdala inputs to ventral CA1-subiculum.
abstract: The hippocampus is essential for learning and memory and interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions. Although the heterogeneity of intrinsic connectivity of hippocampal neurons is well established, the diversity of its extrahippocampal connectivity remains less understood. Such differential connectivity may contribute to functional diversity of hippocampal neurons in specific positions. Ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral subiculum (vSub) form strong reciprocal connections with the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a region critical for emotional and social regulation. Consequently, BLA-vCA1-vSub circuits have been implicated in anxiety-related and social behaviors. However, the functional connectivity from BLA to vCA1-vSub at the cellular and circuit levels is underexplored. To address this, we combined viral tracing with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)-assisted slice electrophysiology to examine BLA projections to vCA1-vSub in mice of either sex. We found that BLA inputs are not uniformly distributed along the transverse axis in vCA1-vSub. Instead, BLA selectively excites pyramidal neurons in distal vCA1-vSub while largely avoiding proximal vCA1 near CA2. BLA terminals strongly excited parvalbumin-expressing interneurons but only weakly recruited a small subset of somatostatin-expressing interneurons, generating robust disynaptic inhibitory synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons. Additionally, the same distal pyramidal neurons that receive BLA excitation also project back to the BLA. These findings reveal that BLA establishes cell-type- and subregion-specific excitatory connections within vCA1-vSub, highlighting a circuit architecture that may underlie functional heterogeneity in ventral hippocampal processing.Significance statement The hippocampus interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions, yet how long-range extrahippocampal inputs are organized across hippocampal subregions remains poorly understood. We examined projections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to the ventral hippocampus and found that BLA inputs selectively excite pyramidal neurons in distal ventral CA1 and ventral subiculum while largely avoiding proximal ventral CA1. BLA projections preferentially excite parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, provide disynaptic inhibition onto pyramidal neurons, and are reciprocally connected with the same pyramidal neurons in ventral CA1 and subiculum they excite. These findings reveal a highly selective connectivity pattern of amygdala-hippocampal circuits, providing a circuit framework for understanding how emotional information is routed through distinct ventral hippocampal pathways.

title: Gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes.
abstract: The information we hold in mind with working memory (WM) may propagate beyond the cortex and out to the peripheral motor system. For instance, directionally biased hand and eye movements can express simple visuo-spatial features during WM maintenance. If such sensorimotor inflections are a form of WM representation, they may also express more detailed and task-adaptive information about WM content. Here, we ask whether gaze patterns carry item-specific detail about complex stimuli held in mind, and whether gaze during WM maintenance adapts to upcoming behavioral demands. To do this, we tracked male and female human eye movements during WM for naturalistic images, and we manipulated which image properties were most task-relevant (visual or semantic). In two experiments, we found that the eyes moved in item-specific spatiotemporal sequences during WM maintenance. Delay period gaze patterns retraced the scanpaths from stimulus encoding, echoing the 'gaze reinstatement' that has been observed during long-term memory retrieval. Therefore, gaze patterns during WM may reinstate visual encoding processes for maintenance. We also used time-resolved representational similarity analyses, guided by convolutional neural network modeling, to test the specificity of WM gaze patterns across a trial. We found that gaze representations were more distinct when the task prioritized visual detail, and they also ramped up in anticipation of the WM probe. Therefore, oculomotor WM signals are malleable to when and how the content will be used. WM may recruit the most primary structures in sensorimotor processing, where eye movements reflect flexible and future-oriented WM content information.Significance Statement The eyes are an outwardly accessible extension of the brain. They filter sensory input and enact motor output, but may also offer a rich window into underlying cognition. For instance, pupil dilation can reflect changing cognitive load, and biased eye movements can reflect basic spatial information about content held in mind with working memory (WM). WM is a critical neuro-cognitive function, but its physiological bases remain under debate. Here, we show that during WM the eyes can move in intricate patterns that read out the complex, real-world stimuli held in mind. This work shows how cognitive states influence oculomotor functions, and also advances theories of WM maintenance to include the most basic structures in sensorimotor processing.

title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI.
abstract: Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation.Significance Statement How quickly does the brain's structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

title: The balance N1 attenuates but persists during self-initiated and repeated perturbations, even without active balance control.
abstract: Standing balance requires rapid responses to postural disturbances, and the balance N1 has been proposed to reflect cortical involvement in corrective motor output. Our recent work shows, however, that the N1 persists even when active balance control is removed and corrective muscle activity is largely absent, suggesting it reflects sensory rather than motor processing. Because the N1 is also modulated by contextual factors such as postural threat, stability, and perturbation predictability, it may reflect uncertainty associated with perturbation-evoked sensory signals. We tested this in 11 participants (3 males and 8 females) using toes-up perturbations across three manipulations expected to alter sensorimotor uncertainty: perturbation timing through 15 unexpected perturbations before and after a block of self-initiated trials; repeated exposure through 60 self-initiated trials; and body-motion variability by comparing active balance with passive support and by imposing prerecorded whole-body motion during 60 additional self-initiated trials with passive support. Self-initiation reduced N1 amplitude by 21.3 ± 13.9% relative to unexpected perturbations, and this attenuation was equivalent across active and passive conditions. Habituation through repeated self-initiated perturbations produced a further 24.0 ± 17.7% decline, again independent of active balance. When perturbations were subsequently delivered unexpectedly, N1 amplitudes increased, confirming that attenuation was specific to the self-initiated context. Finally, imposing prerecorded whole-body motion during passive support did not change perturbation-evoked N1 amplitude, suggesting that body-motion variability does not drive the cortical response when active balance control is absent. These results indicate that the balance N1 is shaped by predictability and repetition, consistent with prediction error or surprise-based accounts of cortical responses to balance perturbations.Significance statement The balance N1, a cortical response to postural disturbances, has long been thought to reflect corrective motor output. We recently showed it instead reflects sensory processing, as it persists even without active balance control. Here we test whether this processing scales with uncertainty associated with perturbation-evoked sensory signals by manipulating perturbation timing through self-initiation, habituation through repeated exposure, and variability of ongoing whole-body motion. Self-initiation and repetition both attenuated N1, regardless of whether participants actively balanced or were passively supported. However, increasing whole-body motion variability did not modify the response, indicating that not all sources of uncertainty modulate the N1. These findings recast the balance N1 as tracking the sensory predictability of the perturbation, not balance-correcting motor output.

abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 1 . Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model 2,3 . Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor—encapsulated within a GalNAc–lipid nanoparticle—leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 ( ANGPTL3 ), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

abstract: Structural and functional insights into the mouse hypothalamus are hampered by its small size and deep location. Here, we leverage ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging (UHF-MRI) at 17.2 Tesla to achieve high spatial resolution in structural, functional and neurochemical imaging of the mouse hypothalamus. From high-resolution- ex vivo anatomical data we created the MRI HypoAtlas, which improves on existing resources and reveals hypothalamic nuclei previously unresolved by MRI. Diffusion MRI and tractography mapped intra- and extra-hypothalamic pathways, facilitating circuit-level exploration without a priori assumptions. Resting-state fMRI combined with independent component analysis identified novel hypothalamic networks, demonstrating the enhanced capacity of UHF-MRI to detect deep-brain activity. ¹H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy quantified neurochemical profiles, revealing sexually dimorphic heterogeneity within the hypothalamus. Our comprehensive multimodal approach uncovered sex differences in hypothalamic anatomy, microstructure and neurochemistry, supporting the added value of these methodological advances. This integrated study offers a valuable resource for dissecting hypothalamic circuits and functions and ultimately advancing our understanding of neuroendocrine regulation, behavior and disease mechanisms, with direct translational relevance.

abstract: Patient access to nutritious food is critical for managing cardiometabolic conditions, yet barriers persist in under-resourced populations. This pilot randomized controlled trial ( N = 210) evaluated the impact of medically tailored groceries (MTG) and food resource coaching (Coach) delivered via a co-located food pantry. Participants with Type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemias, and/or hypertension were recruited from a safety-net health center and received either usual pantry support, MTG, or MTG+Coach for four months. Exploratory outcomes reported herein include self-reported diet quality, food security, and perceived health; blood pressure (BP) from electronic health records ( N = 166). Additional exploratory self-reported outcomes recommended by the funder and detailed in the supplemental materials include nutrition security, wellbeing (EQ-5D-51), loneliness, adaptive capacity, and the Cooking and Food Provisioning Action Scale. Follow-up completion was 81%. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health ( P < 0.001), but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between MTG arms and usual pantry support for any exploratory outcome. Although descriptively larger BP reductions were observed in the intervention groups, confidence intervals were wide and adjusted between-group comparisons were not statistically significant. Further studies with standardized clinical measurement are warranted. Trial registration: This trial and protocol were submitted to ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06242808) on February 3 rd , 2024, prior to recruitment.

abstract: The human brain organizes visual processing into spatially structured functional clusters. Recent topographic neural networks model category-selective clusters but are limited to static images and ventral cortex. In this work, we model the topographic organization of dynamic visual representations across high-level visual cortex. We introduce a general method that spatially arranges and transforms units from a neural network onto a simulated cortical sheet. Applied to a pretrained video foundation model, the method produces spatially structured response correlations while preserving task performance and brain alignment. It captures ventral and dorsal clusters, including face-, body-, and motion-selective patches, and reflects system-level selectivity distributions for animacy, object size, and static versus dynamic content. Functional selectivity varies smoothly across both model and human tissue, suggesting predominantly general-purpose cortical processing with continuous transitions into local functional clusters. Taken together, we provide a computational framework for understanding the spatial and functional organization of high-level visual cortex.

abstract: Persistent activation of cardiac fibroblasts drives excessive extracellular matrix deposition, promoting maladaptive myocardial fibrosis, adverse remodeling, and heart failure (HF) progression. Although Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) and Aortic carboxypeptidase-like protein (ACLP, full-length protein coded by AEBP1 ) have been implicated in pathological fibrosis across multiple organs, including the heart, its functional role in cardiac fibrosis remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that AEBP1 is a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling. Fibroblast-specific knockout or myocardial knockdown of Aebp1 significantly improves cardiac function and prevents pathological remodeling in murine models of myocardial ischemia and pressure-overload induced injury. In human myocardial tissue culture studies, ACLP overexpression induces pathological remodeling in non-failing hearts, whereas AEBP1 knockdown induces structural reverse remodeling in failing myocardium. Mechanistically, ACLP regulates the expression of MRTFB, RUNX2, SM22 and COL1A1, thereby orchestrating fibroblast activation. Collectively, these findings identify AEBP1 as a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and highlights its inhibition as a potential anti-fibrotic therapy following acute injury.

abstract: The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells.

abstract: A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.

abstract: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause diseases ranging from gastroenteritis to typhoid fever. Using live-imaging with controlled-polarity human intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) organoids, we identify epithelial cell sensing as a pre-invasion stage of infection. The generalist serovar Typhimurium migrates toward apical but away from basolateral IEC surfaces, whereas the human-restricted serovar Typhi exhibits the opposite behavior. This polarized tropism is coordinated by signaling between the Aer and Tcp chemoreceptors. Tcp senses citrate released from apical IEC surfaces, while Aer differentially integrates this signal. A single conserved, serovar-specific residue in Aer determines whether Tcp-dependent citrate sensing promotes attraction or repulsion. This pre-invasion stage directs Salmonella to IEC surfaces permissive for invasion and contributes to distinct invasion outcomes. Our findings define a serovar-specific strategy for IEC surface recognition and provide mechanistic insight into how S . Typhimurium and S . Typhi differentially initiate interactions with the human intestinal epithelium.

abstract: The role of the hippocampus in resolving memory interference has been greatly elucidated by considering the relationship between the similarity of visual stimuli (input) and corresponding similarity of hippocampal activity patterns (output). However, these input-output functions can take surprisingly different forms. Here, we reconcile seemingly conflicting findings by considering the possibility that the hippocampus prioritizes different dimensions of visual similarity across different stages of learning. First, we generated a set of natural scene images from two visual categories and rigorously characterized visual similarity using a wide array of methods: neural networks, artificial intelligence models, and human perceptual and memory decisions. We then identified two orthogonal dimensions of visual similarity that each predicted memory interference, but that did so at distinct stages of learning. Using high-resolution fMRI, we then tested for dimension-specific input-output functions within the hippocampus. Within CA3 and dentate gyrus (CA3/DG), we show that dimensions of visual similarity were inverted (repulsion) at stages of learning when they contributed to memory interference. In contrast, CA3/DG preserved similarity when dimensions did not contribute to interference. These findings reveal that hippocampal representations of visually-similar stimuli are highly dynamic and critically depend on the dimensions of similarity that currently contribute to memory interference.

abstract: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during endovascular treatment (EVT) may increase first-pass recanalization and dissolve microcirculatory thrombi, but its efficacy and safety are uncertain. We hypothesised that this strategy would improve functional outcomes versus EVT alone. This phase 3, randomised, adaptive-enrichment, open-label, blinded-endpoint multicentre study aims to evaluate whether intra‑arterial tenecteplase improves clinical outcomes for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Patients with large‑vessel occlusion eligible for EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1) to the tenecteplase group receiving intra‑arterial tenecteplase during EVT or the control group receiving EVT alone. The primary endpoint was favorable functional outcome. Of 380 randomised patients (192 in the tenecteplase group and 188 in the control group), primary outcome data were available for 190 and 186 patients, respectively. Favorable 90-day functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) occurred in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 46.8% of the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 0.76, [95% CI 0.50–1.14], P = 0.19). This work suggests intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy did not improve 90-day functional outcomes in this population. abstract: The clinical effect of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase after successful recanalization in acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) remains uncertain. In this prospective, randomized, adaptive-enrichment, open label, blinded-end point, multi-center trial, patients with BAO within 24 h of estimated symptom onset who achieved successful reperfusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) were randomized (1:1) to intra-arterial tenecteplase ( n = 75) or control (only received standard medical therapy, n = 69). The primary efficacy outcome was independent ambulation (modified Rankin Scale 0–3) at 90 days; the primary safety outcome was symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH). The trial was stopped early due to safety concerns and lack of efficacy per Data Safety and Monitoring Committee recommendation. Among 144 randomized patients, 143 (99.3%) completed follow-up. At 90 days, independent ambulation was achieved in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 50.0% in the control group (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.34–1.29; P = 0.23). sICH occurred in 6.2% versus 4.8% (OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.28–6.89; P = 0.73). All-cause mortality at 90 days was 41.3% versus 26.5% (OR 1.96; 95% CI 0.97–4.03; P = 0.063). In this prematurely terminated trial, adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase did not improve functional outcomes in patients with BAO.

abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. Although the rumen microbiome is central to nitrogen turnover, the role of small peptides, a critical nitrogen pool, remains poorly understood. Here, we constructed a genome-resolved atlas of predicted small-peptide metabolism and integrated high-performance chemical isotope-labeling metabolomics with metagenomics in 30 dairy cows. Among 349 detected small peptides, proline-containing dipeptides were associated with higher NUE, together with an S15 peptidyl-peptidase with Xaa–Pro dipeptide-generating activity. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Bacterial incubation and heterologous expression confirmed that S15.001 hydrolyzed Xaa–Pro substrates. These findings identify a microbial proline-dipeptide axis associated with NUE and provide a basis for precision nutrition strategies targeting ruminal peptide metabolism.

abstract: The epithelial barrier serves as a critical defense against bacterial invasion that is traditionally thought to be disrupted by transcriptional or proteolytic turnover of adherens junctions. Here, we reveal a striking, non-canonical mechanism of barrier failure in which the transcription factor FOXO1 mediates rapid bacteria-induced loss of barrier function independent of gene transcription or proteolysis. Using a 3D microfluidic device and an in vivo murine model, we demonstrate that bacteria or lipopolysaccharide trigger dramatic relocalization of FOXO1 to the nucleus with subsequent redistribution of E-cadherin from the membrane to the cytoplasm, resulting in an increase in epithelial leakiness. Furthermore, we found that stimulation increased FOXO1 binding to β-catenin and enhanced β-catenin Tyr654 phosphorylation, which were accompanied by disruption of the β-catenin–E-cadherin complex and destabilization of epithelial barrier integrity. Nuclear-restricted FOXO1 expression alone is sufficient to replicate bacterial effects and induce barrier failure, while cytoplasmic retention or epithelial-specific Foxo1 deletion rescues barrier function and preserves membrane-localized E-cadherin and β-catenin despite bacterial challenge. These findings define a FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin spatiotemporal axis as a previously unrecognized rapid-response mechanism controlling epithelial barrier integrity.

abstract: Neutrophil extracellular trap formation is a central innate immune defence mechanism that depends on NADPH oxidase–driven reactive oxygen species production. How NADP⁺ availability is regulated during neutrophil activation remains unclear. Using integrated lipidomic, biochemical and functional analyses in human neutrophils, we identify NAD kinase, the sole enzyme responsible for NADP⁺ synthesis, as a direct lipid-regulated effector downstream of phospholipase D1. Neutrophil activation induces rapid, phospholipase D1-dependent production of phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which bind and activate NAD kinase. The resulting cytosolic NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and consumed by NADPH oxidase during neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of phospholipase D1 suppresses NAD kinase activity, depletes NADP⁺ and impairs neutrophil extracellular trap formation independently of direct NADPH oxidase inhibition. These findings define a lipid–metabolic axis coupling phospholipase D1-driven membrane remodelling to NADP⁺ availability and innate immune function.
